title: Show what you can do at work

heads: What makes an application statement believable?
Connect the employer’s task with the applicant’s action
Build a short context–action–result statement
prose: A first application can use school or community experience. The task is to show a relevant action truthfully, so an employer can see why it relates to the work being advertised.

A job posting is an employer’s advertisement for an opening. A duty is work the person would do. An experience record describes what the applicant has already done. These documents have different jobs: one states what is needed; the other supplies possible evidence.

A quality claim names a characteristic, such as “careful” or “helpful.” An observable action tells a reader what happened, such as “checked the names against the list.” A claim becomes more credible when the action fits it.

Context explains where and why the action mattered. Action names what the person did. Result states what happened afterwards. For a simple example: “During a club event, I checked the room number against the booking sheet and corrected the notice. Visitors reached the booked room.” This could support a checking duty; it does not establish professional management experience.

Match a posting requirement → find a record entry showing a relevant action → explain the context, action and supplied result → remove anything the record does not establish. An applicant can contribute to a team result without claiming to have done everyone’s work.

When you read the case: Next you will meet Rowan, read the employer’s notice and inspect Rowan’s preparation notes. Look first for the work the employer actually needs; then select an action that shows Rowan doing something relevant. The later sections demonstrate and support the writing.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Rowan is applying for a first job
prose: Prairie Library Hub runs Saturday activities for families. It needs someone at the welcome desk to greet visitors, explain how to sign in and help keep its records accurate. Rowan would like this job but has never been paid to work in a library.
An application is a request to be considered for a job. In this lesson, the employer asks applicants for a short written example of relevant experience.

Rowan has helped at school and community events. Those experiences may show skills the library needs. The challenge is to choose a useful example and explain it honestly, instead of simply writing “I would be good at this job.”

Your role: help Rowan prepare a short application response. You will read the employer’s advertisement, find a matching experience in Rowan’s notes and write as Rowan using “I.” You do not need to supply your own work history.
First, find out what the employer needs. Then look at what Rowan has already done.

heads: What is a job posting?
prose: A job posting is an advertisement an employer uses to find someone for a job. It usually tells you the job title, the work involved, qualifications or skills, practical details such as hours, and how to apply. Its duties are the tasks the successful applicant would do.
At this hub, signing in means recording that you have arrived. Reservation records list the people who have booked a place in an activity.

Read this practice notice in two passes. First, use the title and hours to understand the role. Then read “What you will do.” Those duties tell Rowan which experiences would be useful in an application.
The posting tells us what the library needs. It does not tell us whether Rowan can do it. For that, we need an example from Rowan’s past experience.

heads: What has Rowan already done?
prose: Before applying, Rowan made notes about three school and community activities. These are experience notes: a way to remember what happened and choose examples for an application. They are not an employer’s form or a list of job requirements.

For each activity, notice the situation, what Rowan did and what happened afterwards. You will use these details to support a claim about a skill. A paid job is not the only place someone can practise a skill.
You now have both sides of the application: the employer’s duties and Rowan’s experiences. Next, learn how to connect them in a sentence the employer can understand.

heads: Show the action behind a skill
Use three parts to make the example clear
prose: A skill is an ability someone uses to do a task. For example, explaining instructions is a communication skill. An employer cannot tell how Rowan communicates from the sentence “I am a good communicator.” That sentence makes a claim but gives no example.

That specific example is evidence: information supporting a claim. It must also fit the duty. Explaining sign-in roles is relevant to explaining the library’s sign-in process. Checking an attendance list is more relevant to keeping reservation records accurate.
A result does not have to be a number or an award. “The table opened on time” is a useful result because it tells the employer the preparation was completed when needed.

Describe the original setting accurately. A school example can show a skill that could be used at work, but it does not become library experience. If an example involves other people’s information, describe the task without including their names or private records.
The demonstration below uses the welcome-evening notes. Watch how the writer chooses one duty, selects the matching action and turns it into a short application response.

title: Make decisions on a first shift

heads: Know the difference between a task and permission to do it
Read responsibility, authorization and training separately
Choose a permitted step and a clear message
prose: A first-shift sheet explains the work and its limits. Before using it to make decisions, distinguish what a helper is responsible for, what they are allowed to do and what they need to learn.

A responsibility is something a role is expected to do. Authorization is permission for a particular action. Training is instruction and practice needed to carry it out. Being asked to help at a desk does not automatically authorize changing a reservation or using unfamiliar equipment.
A boundary identifies what must stay protected, such as accurate records, private participant information or people’s safety. A task can be familiar while a particular action still needs approval.

First identify the situation and relevant boundary. If information or permission is missing, pause that action. Use a safe, permitted task while waiting only when doing so does not leave an immediate hazard unattended. A floor plan can help locate a clear route and the responsible person.

For a simple example, an unready login is a reason to leave the record unchanged and ask for the approved access process. “The login is not ready; I have left the record unchanged. Can you show me the approved process?” identifies the problem, action already taken and needed response.
Use notice → boundary → safe permitted action → specific message → required instruction or approval. The supplied brief determines who may authorize work in these cases.

When you read the case: Read the shift brief and floor plan for permission labels, privacy rules, safe routes and contact information. The first check asks which task is already permitted. The later cases ask you to use the same boundaries when something is uncertain or unsafe.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Helpful work includes knowing when to pause
prose: Rowan has been given a first-shift sheet at Prairie Library Hub, a fictional community activity space. Some tasks can begin immediately; others require a demonstration or permission. Rowan wants to help without guessing about records, equipment or people's information.

You will use the sheet and floor plan to make a decision, explain its basis and write a precise message. At the end, you will complete two decision rows for a changed situation. This is an online simulation: you make decisions from the supplied documents, not by doing actual workplace tasks.

How to complete this lesson: Read Rowan's first-shift folder before answering the document check. Learn Read permission and responsibility together, then follow the reservation example. Try Three moments at the desk and revise with feedback. Answer six understanding questions and complete The spray and the information request. Review your two rows, check the criteria and choose Complete lesson. You can pause after the guided decisions; all work saves.

heads: Rowan's first-shift folder
Read the floor plan
prose: Rowan is a new helper. Morgan is the shift lead: the person assigned to explain tasks and approve work in this case. Rowan's shift is Monday, 9 a.m.–1 p.m. The first stop is the welcome desk. A shift brief is a short set of instructions for that working period; it is not evidence that the new worker already knows every task.
Prairie Library Hub — first-shift sheet
Start now: welcome visitors, prepare blank activity cards and restock public brochures.
Wait for Morgan: do not open or change reservation records until Morgan provides an approved individual login and demonstrates the process. Never use another person's login.

Spill or blocked route: stay on a safe, dry route; keep people away from the hazard, place the available cone only if this can be done without entering the hazard, and notify Morgan immediately. Do not attempt cleanup with an unfamiliar product or leave people walking into the hazard. The front-desk extension reaches Morgan without Rowan leaving the desk. The cone is within reach on the dry side of the welcome desk.

Private information: keep participant details face down in the secure desk tray when not being used. Do not share another participant's details. Ask Morgan to handle requests through the approved process.

Equipment: the supply cart may be moved along the clear route if stable and safe to move. One closed cleaning spray is labelled “Training required before use.” Rowan has not received that training. Permission to move the cart is not permission to use its contents.

The public entrance leads to the welcome desk. The brochure shelf is beyond the desk. Morgan is in the activity room. A spill blocks the shorter route across the open area. The marked clear route goes around the spill to the activity-room entrance. The cleaning cart is beside the blocked route. The extension and secure tray are at the welcome desk.
[Place the approved library floor-plan image here, followed by the same text description above.]

heads: Read permission and responsibility together
Pause the uncertain task and choose useful permitted work
Make the message actionable
prose: A responsibility is something the role is expected to do. Authorization is permission to perform a particular action. Training is instruction and practice needed to carry it out appropriately. The three are related but not interchangeable. Rowan is responsible for helping at the desk; that does not authorize every action available on its computer.

A boundary tells you what must remain protected while you act. The reservation boundary protects accurate records and controlled access. The information boundary protects participant details. The hazard boundary protects people from entering a dangerous area. A useful response identifies the relevant boundary rather than simply saying “be careful.”

Pausing one action does not mean abandoning the whole shift. If record access is not ready, Rowan can prepare blank cards or welcome visitors within the brief. If a spill is present, protecting people and contacting Morgan takes priority over routine preparation. The safest immediate step depends on the situation; “do another task” would not be enough if people were still walking into a spill.

The floor plan helps with this choice. It identifies a clear route and a way to contact Morgan without crossing the spill. A diagram is useful when its locations affect action. Here, choosing the short route would contradict the hazard information even if it saved time.

A good short message contains the location or task, the specific uncertainty or risk, what you have done within permission and what you need confirmed. Compare “I need help” with “The reservation login is not ready; I have left the record unchanged. Can you show me the approved process?” The second message allows Morgan to respond to a concrete need.

Decision sequence: notice the situation → identify the boundary → take a safe permitted step → give a specific message → wait for the needed instruction before the restricted task. Do not turn a plausible guess into permission.

CCOHS reference record — retrieved September 28, 2026; fact sheet confirmed current June 30, 2025: the right to know includes receiving hazard information and necessary instruction before work. In Rowan's case, the training label is a reason to ask before using the spray. The shift sheet supplies the actual case procedure. Optional “Three Rights of Workers,” Right to Know.

heads: Reservation access is not ready
prose: At 9:10, a visitor asks Rowan to change a reservation. Morgan has not provided an individual login or a demonstration. A co-worker offers a logged-in computer. No immediate hazard is present in this particular moment.

I locate the relevant rule: reservation records must wait for approved access and a demonstration, and another person's login is prohibited. The co-worker's offer does not change those instructions. Rowan can acknowledge the visitor without promising an unauthorized change.
Completed decision row

After the request is safely handed to Morgan, Rowan can prepare blank cards while waiting. “Use the co-worker's login, then tell Morgan later” reverses the required order and removes accountability for the change. Being helpful includes respecting the limit and keeping the visitor informed.

title: Practise a truthful interview

heads: How to answer an interview question with evidence
Choose an experience that answers the question
Own the action and share the result accurately
prose: An interview explores how a person’s preparation fits a role. This lesson uses written rehearsal, so you can learn to explain an experience clearly without a live interview or recording.

A behavioural question asks how someone acted in a situation, for example, “Tell me about a time a plan changed.” Identify the skill being explored, then choose a record containing that kind of event. An unrelated achievement does not explain how the person handled change.

Give the situation and responsibility, describe the person’s own actions, and finish with the supplied result. You can add learning where it helps. The structure is a guide to meaning; you do not have to say its labels in the answer.

A contribution is the person’s part in the work. A team result belongs to everyone who helped. In a simple example, “I checked the supply list; another helper packed the boxes; together we finished before opening” explains both. “I completed everything alone” would change the evidence.

A limit marks what the example cannot prove. One event does not establish years of professional experience. Rehearse by reading as if the listener knows nothing about the event: can they identify the problem, personal action and result?

Use question → relevant experience → personal responsibility and action → result → learning or next question. A focused employer question can ask about training or duties without claiming a conversation has already occurred.

When you read the case: Read the role brief and experience records to distinguish Rowan’s own action from what another helper or the whole team did. The first check asks which description matches Rowan’s contribution. Later you will turn that evidence into an interview answer.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Let the interviewer hear what you actually did
prose: An interview is a conversation used to explore whether a person's experience and a role's needs fit. A general claim such as “I work well under pressure” gives the listener little to examine. A short, accurate example gives them actions, results and something useful to ask about.

You will prepare answers for Rowan using supplied fictional experience notes. Your final product is a 4–6 sentence answer about a disagreement, followed by a role-research question and a sensible way to investigate it. You may rehearse aloud or read silently; no recording, live partner or real interview is required.

How to complete this lesson: Read The role and Rowan's event notes. Learn Build an answer a listener can follow. Follow the cancellation example, then practise with the activity-card mix-up. Check six ideas and complete Answer a question about disagreement. Compare your answer with the annotated model, revise and sign off. Pause after rehearsal if useful; the written fields save.

heads: The role and Rowan's event notes
prose: Rowan is preparing for a fictional welcome-helper interview. The role involves explaining sign-in steps, keeping attendance information accurate, sharing tasks and asking the shift lead when an exception needs approval. Training is provided for the local system. The notice does not state which career qualification could lead to a later program-coordinator role.

An experience record is a description of an event already completed. It is evidence for an answer, not a script Rowan must pretend happened in a paid job. These events took place at school or in a volunteer setting. Use that context truthfully.
Record A — cancelled helper, school welcome evening

Ten minutes before doors opened, one of three helpers could not attend. Rowan was responsible for organizing the sign-in table. Rowan asked the remaining helper to check the attendance list, took the greeting position and explained the revised two-person arrangement to the event lead. The lead approved it. Arrivals moved through without a long line, and every arrival was recorded. After the event Rowan wrote, “Next time I would prepare a backup task plan before opening.”
Record B — mixed activity cards, community open house

Two stacks of activity cards had been placed under the wrong headings. Rowan noticed the mismatch before visitors used them, checked the approved activity list with the lead and relabelled the stacks with the lead's confirmation. A second helper distributed them. Visitors received the intended card for their activity. Rowan has used this local list once; the record does not establish expertise with every registration system.

heads: Build an answer a listener can follow
Own your action and share the result
Practise the delivery and prepare a useful question
prose: A behavioural question asks for an example of how someone acted, such as “Tell me about a time a plan changed.” Start by identifying the skill the question is exploring. A question about change needs an event involving change; an unrelated achievement may be impressive but fail to answer it.

Give enough situation and task for the listener to understand the problem and your responsibility. Then spend most of the answer on action: what you personally did and why. Finish with the result, limited to what the record actually reports. You can add learning or a next step when it helps. This structure is a guide for meaning, not a requirement to say the words “situation, task, action, result” aloud.

Answer path: what happened → what I was responsible for → what I did → what changed → what I learned or would improve. In a short answer, one sentence can contain more than one part. A precise action often communicates more than several adjectives.

Teamwork creates a common wording trap. “We kept the line moving” credits the group but does not identify Rowan's contribution. “I did all the work” supplies a contribution by inventing one. Combine them: “I took greeting and arranged the task split; together we kept arrivals moving and recorded everyone.” The result can be shared while the action remains specific.

A limit marks what an example cannot prove. One local event does not establish years of professional management, and following an approved procedure does not establish qualification to design a new system. Naming a sensible limit strengthens the evidence instead of weakening it.

Rehearsal helps you notice long openings, missing verbs and unexplained results. Read your answer once as if a listener knows nothing about the event. If speaking is useful to you, say it aloud without recording. If you prefer silent rehearsal, underline the action and identify the result in the text. Both routes check the same content; accent, eye contact and performance style are not scored here.

Networking means building professional connections to exchange information and learn about opportunities. It need not begin with asking for a job. A career event, a workplace information session or a short informational conversation can help a person understand a role. A focused question respects the other person's time: “What training lets a welcome helper take on program coordination?” is more useful than “Tell me everything about your career.” In this course, you draft the question and choose an appropriate route; you do not contact anyone.

A mentor is someone who shares experience and feedback to support another person's development. Mentoring is a relationship, not a credential or a guarantee of an opportunity. An internship is an organized period of work-related learning; its actual duties, supervision, training, pay and entry conditions must be checked in its own agreement. A mock interview rehearses interview questions before a real selection process. This lesson provides that rehearsal in writing. Preparing a question for a mentor or employer is different from claiming that a conversation or internship has already happened.

heads: Tips for Your Résumé
prose: This excerpt discusses written applications: a résumé summarizes facts, while a cover letter explains relevance. You will transfer that idea to an interview answer. Listen for why specific accomplishments matter, then look back at Rowan’s school and community records.
FINLIT 101 · Tips for Your Résumé · selected excerpt, used with permission.
This short practice check saves with your lesson work. You can change your answer after reading the feedback.

heads: “Tell me about a time a plan changed.”
prose: Record A directly answers this question: a helper cancelled shortly before opening. I need only one sentence of background. Rowan's response is the important part, so I name the task split and approval. The recorded result is a moving line and complete attendance, not a numerical increase in efficiency that nobody measured.

Complete answer: “At a school welcome evening, a helper cancelled ten minutes before opening while I was organizing sign-in. I asked the remaining helper to check the attendance list and took the greeting position myself. I explained the revised arrangement to the event lead and received approval. Together we kept arrivals moving without a long line and recorded everyone. Next time I would prepare a backup task plan before opening.”

How the answer works: sentence 1 provides situation and responsibility; sentences 2–3 identify Rowan's actions and authority; sentence 4 credits the team result; sentence 5 uses the recorded improvement. It does not imply that Rowan supervised paid staff or handled an unknown computer system.

title: Work through a changing shift

heads: How to change a work plan when something blocks it
Identify blockers and dependencies
Report early and check the remaining time
prose: A changed shift needs an updated order of actions. A deadline matters, but permission, training, safety and privacy still govern the response.

A blocker prevents a task from progressing as planned. An alternative is another way to achieve the purpose. A dependency is a step that must happen before another can begin. If a supervisor must approve a location, approval comes before moving the activity there.

A priority depends on consequences and order. Immediate safety and privacy needs take attention before routine tasks. Parallel work happens at the same time, but it requires available people or resources; one person cannot perform two separate hands-on tasks simultaneously.

A useful update states the time, blocker, affected deadline and request. For a simple example: “The copier stopped at 9:00; notices are needed by 10:00. May I prepare the approved blank version?” This lets the responsible person decide before the delay grows.

Work backwards from the deadline. A 15-minute task due at 10:00 must start by 9:45. Then check whether permission and earlier steps can finish in time. Doing unapproved work quickly does not make the plan valid.

Use protect people and information → report → identify approval and dependencies → assign workable tasks and times → check the deadline. A successful finish can still leave a process improvement worth recording.

When you read the case: Read the supplied shift rules before judging the incident. Locate who approves alternatives and which steps must precede setup. The first reading check asks about that authority; the later tasks add time and changing conditions.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: A changed plan needs a new order of actions
prose: During a busy shift, an equipment problem can affect a deadline while visitors still need help. Working faster on the original list may not solve the new problem. You will practise deciding what must stop, what can continue and what the shift lead needs to know.

Your final product is a timed decision log for a room change. It will name a first action, protect private information, use an approved alternative and explain one improvement from earlier feedback. All events are supplied simulations; no physical setup, supervised placement or contact with a real workplace is required.

How to complete this lesson: Read The printer incident and the shift rules, then check who can approve an alternative. Learn Replan without guessing, follow the revised printer response, and practise The outdoor change. After six questions, complete A room becomes unavailable. Compare the model and times, revise and sign off. Pause after the outdoor practice if needed; your work saves.

heads: The printer incident and the shift rules
prose: Rowan helps at fictional Prairie Library Hub. Morgan leads the shift. A blocker is a condition that prevents a task from progressing as planned. An alternative is a different way to reach the purpose; it still needs to meet the rules.
Desk rules for these cases
Completed incident record — Monday, September 14

At 10:05 the printer stopped. Cards were needed for an 11:00 activity. Rowan spent fifteen minutes trying to get printing working and notified Morgan at 10:20. At 10:25 Morgan approved blank cards with handwritten activity headings; preparing them took twenty minutes, and the cards were ready at 10:45. No private information was needed on the cards. The activity began on time.

Morgan's noon feedback: “The cards were accurate and ready, but I needed to know about the printer at 10:05. An early message would have given us more time to choose a backup. Please report a blocker when you first notice it.”

heads: Replan without guessing
Communicate the problem before it becomes a surprise
Use time as evidence
prose: A priority is something that needs attention before another task. Priority depends on consequence and sequence, not just on which request is loudest. Immediate safety and privacy boundaries continue to apply when a deadline changes. After protecting those boundaries, identify the task whose delay would block other work.

A dependency is a step that must happen before another can begin. Location approval and an area check are dependencies for setting up in a new room. Writing a draft public notice can happen while waiting, but posting an unapproved location would skip a dependency. This difference lets a person stay useful without pretending approval has arrived.

A concise update gives a time, blocker, consequence and request. “Printer stopped at 10:05; cards are needed by 11. May I use blank cards with the activity headings?” gives Morgan information for a decision. An early message does not require Rowan to know the cause of the failure. Reporting a problem and offering an option are compatible with taking initiative.

The original incident ended on time, but the feedback still identifies a process worth changing. A successful result does not prove every step was effective. Conversely, one late report does not prove Rowan is generally unreliable. Keep the improvement specific: report blockers when noticed and name the affected deadline.

Work backwards from the deadline. If a task takes ten minutes and must finish at 10:45, it must start by 10:35. If approval cannot arrive until 10:25, check whether the remaining sequence still fits. Activities that can occur at the same time must be assigned to different available people; one person cannot independently perform two ten-minute tasks simultaneously.
Replanning map: protect people and information → report the change → identify permissions and dependencies → assign feasible tasks and times → check the deadline → record the next improvement.

Optional training reference, read September 28, 2026: CCOHS explains that workers need information and instruction about hazards before the work. In this lesson, that supports waiting for an authorized area check; the fictional desk rules determine who is authorized. “Right to Know”.

heads: Improve the printer response
prose: We are looking back at September 14, not rewriting what actually happened. The incident record says Rowan reported at 10:20. The model below proposes what Rowan could do at 10:05 in a similar future situation.

First, stop repeated repair attempts. The rules allow a normal safe restart, not dismantling or a fifteen-minute delay before reporting. The deadline is 11:00, and the purpose is readable activity headings, not printing for its own sake. Blank cards might meet that purpose, but Morgan must approve the change.
Improved decision log

This is a complete response even though Rowan does not diagnose the printer. “Fix the mechanism quickly” requires skills and permission not supplied. “The activity started on time, so no change is needed” ignores the feedback about avoidable pressure.

title: Check the rules before a first shift

heads: How to check an employment rule against a shift
Know what the documents establish
Match the facts before deciding
prose: A rule can apply differently depending on a worker’s age, employment arrangement, tasks and hours. This lesson teaches how to connect the supplied facts with the relevant row in an official-rule record.

An employee works for an employer. An employment standard is a minimum employment rule in the applicable system. Jurisdiction identifies which rules or authority apply. For these cases, read the supplied Alberta youth-employment record rather than applying a general idea about all teen work.

A permit is official permission for specified employment. Parent or guardian consent is a different condition. Adult supervision means an adult supervises the work as described in the record; another worker’s experience or an adult’s reachable telephone number does not establish that condition.

Use age → employment arrangement → workplace and task → day and time to locate the relevant rule. Separate a shift where supervision or the calendar day changes. One condition being met does not cancel another condition: for example, permission cannot be assumed to remove a stated hours restriction.

A mismatch is a supplied fact conflicting with a rule. An unknown is a relevant fact not supplied. State a mismatch with the matching rule; ask a specific question for an unknown. Keep personal constraints, such as transport, distinct from rules applying to a group of workers.

For a simple reading example, a rule requiring adult coverage until closing needs evidence about who covers the final portion of the shift. “An adult supervises the opening” leaves a different question unanswered.

When you read the case: Read the worker record, draft offer and dated rule record together. Locate the supervisor’s age and coverage times before the first check. All rules and facts needed here are supplied; the task is a fictional source-based review rather than a real employment determination.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

A shift offer can sound simple: “Can you close on Thursday?” To check it, a young worker needs more than the finish time. Age, workplace, school hours, tasks, permission and supervision can change which rules apply.

You will help Ellis check a proposed retail shift, practise checking a corrected offer, and then write a shift-review note for a different restaurant worker. Your final note will connect particular facts to particular rules and propose a workable next step. You are practising source-based investigation, not issuing a legal decision about a real employer.

Work through Meet the situation and read the documents → Use the method with the case → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Pause after the example or guided practice if useful. Your answers save automatically. Guided work and six questions are practice; the independent review note is your saved lesson evidence.

Useful terms. An employee works for an employer; the youth rules below concern employees. A permit is official permission for specified employment, not the same as a parent's consent. Retail sells goods, including food, directly to customers. Supervision means an adult is actually supervising the work; being able to telephone someone elsewhere is not the supervision supplied in our examples. A school day is a day on which this learner is scheduled to attend school.

Optional reference disclosure: Official pages for a current situation. The dated record below contains everything needed here. For an actual job, check the current Alberta youth employment page and use Employment Standards' question service if the situation differs. You do not need to open a website, contact anyone or enter personal employment details to finish this lesson.

heads: Document A — Worker and school record
Document B — Draft shift offer, received October 5
Document C — In-course Alberta youth employment record
Read the documents
prose: Ellis is starting an ordinary employee job at fictional North Path Books, an Alberta retail bookstore. Ellis wants to answer a shift offer before it becomes the final schedule. Read the worker record, offer and rule record together: none is enough by itself.
Jordan is experienced, but is not an adult. Ellis has not accepted or worked this proposed shift.

Government of Alberta, “Employment standards rules – Youth employment laws”; relevant sections “Basic rules,” “Employees 13 to 14 years of age,” and “Employees 15 to 17 years of age.” Checked September 28, 2026. Limited paraphrase for this lesson:

This selected record does not list every permitted occupation or every employment rule. Permission does not erase an hours restriction. Meeting these selected rules does not establish that all employment and safety requirements have been met.

A 15-year-old cannot work during regular school hours except in an off-campus education program. Age 15–17, retail/hospitality Work from 9:00 p.m. to midnight requires adult supervision. Work from 12:01 a.m. to 6:00 a.m. is prohibited. Age 13–14 Parent/guardian consent is required. Specified jobs may be done without a permit; other jobs require one. Food-service work requires continuous adult supervision.

heads: Identify the rule before judging the offer
Divide the shift where a condition changes
Separate a mismatch from an unanswered question
Ask for a specific correction
prose: Start with the details that select a rule: age → employment arrangement → workplace/task → time. “Teen worker” is too broad. Ellis is 15, so the 13–14 school-day two-hour limit is not the rule to apply to Ellis. North Path Books is retail, so the retail evening rule is relevant. An exception for another kind of workplace cannot simply be moved to this one.

An official page is evidence about the rules; a shift offer is evidence about the proposed facts. The task is to connect them. Write “Ellis is scheduled after midnight in retail, which conflicts with the recorded overnight restriction,” rather than “the website says it is bad.” The first sentence lets another reader check your reasoning.
Midnight crosses into the next calendar day. Adult coverage can change before the shift ends. A whole-shift label such as “night work” hides these differences. Break the offered shift into pieces:
The answer to the last question is no under the supplied record. Do not spend time negotiating an adult supervisor for a portion that cannot be scheduled under that rule. Revise the hours themselves.

A mismatch exists when supplied facts conflict with the selected rule: a retail shift continuing to 12:30 a.m. is one here. An unknown exists when the documents do not tell you a relevant fact. Write a question for an unknown instead of assuming its answer. In Ellis's documents, the ages and coverage are supplied, so “maybe Jordan is an adult” is not an unknown.

A check can have several results. The shift is outside the recorded school hours, but that does not cancel the supervision and overnight problems. Conversely, finding one problem does not mean every detail is wrong. State which conditions your evidence answers.

A useful review ends with an action the recipient can understand: a revised start and finish, named adult coverage and confirmation that permission covers those hours. “Fix it” leaves the next decision unclear. You can be direct without accusing someone of deliberate wrongdoing: this is a draft offer and its reason is unknown.
A personal arrangement, such as a ride home, also affects whether the worker can accept. Label it accurately. The parent's 11:00 p.m. pickup is a case constraint, not a province-wide closing rule.
tables: Portion of Ellis's offer What changes? Question to ask 9:30–10:00 p.m. Thursday Mara is supervising Are the evening consent and supervision conditions supplied? 10:00 p.m.–midnight Mara leaves; Jordan is 17 Is an adult supervising? Does parental consent cover the planned finish? 12:01–12:30 a.m. Friday Overnight restricted period Can adult supervision or consent remove this retail prohibition?

prose: I first select the age 15–17 retail rules. Ellis is 15 and the arrangement is ordinary employment. The shift begins after Thursday's school hours. That answers the school-hours question; it does not approve the rest of the shift.

Next I follow the time line. Mara supplies adult supervision only until 10:00 p.m. Jordan is 17, so the offer does not supply the required adult coverage from 10:00 p.m. to midnight. The parent has only consented to an 11:00 p.m. finish, so the offer also exceeds that permission. Finally, the offered 12:30 a.m. finish includes the prohibited 12:01–6:00 a.m. retail period. Neither permission nor adult coverage can make that portion fit the record.
Here is a complete draft review:

“Ellis can work until 12:30 because the parent could give permission” is an unsupported alternative. It treats consent as an override of a prohibition. “Ellis cannot work more than two hours because school is tomorrow” selects the wrong age group's rule and does not use Ellis's actual school-day facts.

title: Stop, identify and control a hazard

heads: Recognize a hazard before choosing a response
Describe a hazard without creating exposure
Choose the immediate safe action first
prose: A workplace request does not supply the knowledge needed to carry it out safely. Before reading the hazard case, learn to separate an observed condition, a possible harm and the information needed to respond.

A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm. Risk concerns the possibility and seriousness of that harm in the circumstances. A control is a measure used to prevent or reduce exposure. An unreadable product label is an observable information gap; it does not identify the substance.

Observation does not require touching, testing or deliberately smelling something unsafe. “The label cannot be read” reports a fact. “Handling it without instructions could cause harm” states the concern. A claim about its exact chemical identity would need evidence the observer may not have.

Use identify → pause and avoid guessing → report and request information or training → reassess using the responsible assessment and required controls. The first response can stop exposure while a competent person decides the final control. Do not select protective equipment for an unknown hazard by guessing.

The right to know connects to hazard information and instruction; the right to participate connects to reporting and safety assessment. Dangerous-work refusal has an applicable threshold and process; the dated Alberta record in this lesson explains them. A concern should be communicated through that process rather than treated as permission to resume on appearance alone.
For a simple example, unfamiliar equipment with a missing instruction is a reason to stay clear, report the gap and ask for approved training—not to experiment to prove whether it is dangerous.

When you read the case: Read the observation, training information and official-process record before deciding what the worker can do. The first check asks which sentence reports the evidence accurately. The four-step image and the later teaching will connect that observation to a response.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

On a first shift, you may want to show that you can handle a task without slowing anyone down. But a request does not supply the information, equipment or training needed to do it safely. Knowing when to pause is a useful workplace skill.

You will help Devin respond to an unidentified cleaning liquid, practise a follow-up when a coworker offers reassurance, and then create a response plan for a different equipment hazard. Your final product explains the observation, immediate action, report and conditions needed before work resumes.

Your route is Meet the situation and read the documents → Use the method with the case → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Read at your own pace; a useful pause is after the example. Responses save automatically. The guided activity and six questions are practice. Only your independent response plan and review sign-offs complete this lesson.

Vocabulary. A hazard is a source or condition that could cause harm. Risk concerns how harm could occur and how serious or likely it might be. A control is a measure that removes or reduces exposure to a hazard. A procedure is an agreed way to do a task safely. A concern report states what was observed and what action is needed. Reporting does not require proving a chemical's identity or a legal violation.

Optional disclosure: Current official sources. The dated Alberta records below are enough for the lesson. Links allow current verification for a real worksite. No external training, contact or login is required here.

Document B — Supplied worksite instructions

Read the documents
prose: Devin is a new employee at fictional Brookside Community Supplies in Alberta. At 4:10 p.m. on October 6, 2026, supervisor Jo asks Devin to clean a work surface beside a storage area. Devin has not started. The site is provincially regulated.
These are fictional site instructions for the scenario. They do not provide a method for handling any real chemical.

Government of Alberta, “Young worker rights and responsibilities,” sections “Workplace safety,” “Job training,” and “Emergency training and equipment”; “Employer responsibilities,” “Overview” and “Employing youth.” Checked September 28, 2026.

Workers have rights to hazard information, participation in safety and refusal of dangerous work. Workers should report unsafe conditions, follow safe procedures and ask for training they lack. Employers must provide the skills, information, competent supervision and safety arrangements needed for the work. Learners still developing the necessary skills require direct supervision by someone who has them. Chemical work requires special training; equipment alone does not replace instruction.
Government of Alberta, “Refuse dangerous work,” “How it works” and “Worker obligations.” Checked September 28, 2026.

At provincially regulated worksites, the refusal right concerns a reasonable belief in an undue hazard: a serious, immediate threat actually observed or experienced. A worker should stop the dangerous work and promptly report what they refuse and why. The employer investigates and addresses it. Unless fixed immediately, an investigation report is provided. Safe alternative work the person can reasonably do may be assigned. Unresolved danger can be taken to Occupational Health and Safety (OHS). Exercising the legal right is protected from reprisal.

This record explains a process; it does not decide that every uncertainty automatically meets the legal threshold. A worker can ask for missing information and training before reaching a legal conclusion.
tables: What the record establishes What it does not establish Jo pointed to a container of liquid with no readable label. Its identity, concentration or hazard classification. The room feels stuffy; Devin does not know whether the ventilation is operating adequately for this product. A measured exposure level or proof that the air is toxic. Devin has not received the product information, chemical-use training or procedure for this cleaning task. Which gloves, ventilation or other controls would be suitable. Jo is helping another worker in the front area. Devin can reach Jo from the clear doorway without handling the container. Permission to improvise while Jo is busy. Devin has not opened, carried, mixed, smelled deliberately or used the liquid. No injury or visible spill is reported in this written case. Any reason to perform spill cleanup.

heads: Describe what you know without testing the hazard
Use rights as practical actions
Choose the immediate action before the final fix
Close the loop
prose: Observation is useful when it makes the concern concrete: a label cannot be read, training has not occurred, or insulation is visibly damaged. You do not need to get closer, touch an object or deliberately smell a substance to make your report more convincing. Information gathering must not create the exposure you are trying to avoid.

Separate the observation from the possible harm. “The product is unidentified” is established. “Using an unidentified product without instructions could expose someone to harm” explains the concern. “This is definitely a poisonous gas” makes a claim the documents cannot support. Cautious wording can be specific and urgent without exaggeration.

The right to know connects to requesting the identity, hazard information, training and procedure. The right to participate connects to reporting the condition and contributing information during its assessment. The right to refuse dangerous work has an Alberta process and threshold, described in Document C. It is more than walking away silently: the employer needs to know which work is being refused and why.

Worker and employer responsibilities fit together. Devin must report and avoid unsafe improvisation. Jo and the employer must arrange appropriate information, assessment, supervision and controls. Devin does not become the chemical expert merely because Devin noticed a problem.

An immediate action keeps exposure from increasing while a competent person works out the fix. For Devin, that means not handling the liquid, staying clear and reaching Jo from the doorway. The final control depends on information Devin does not have. It might involve a verified product, a different task or another trained worker; this lesson cannot select gloves or chemical procedures for an unknown substance.
Use the four-step image as a reminder, with this complete text equivalent:

“Reassess” does not mean giving yourself permission because the room looks normal. Work can resume only when the hazard has been addressed and the worker has the competence and controls required for the assigned work. Replacing Devin with another equally untrained person merely transfers the concern.

A useful handoff identifies who will act, what must be checked and how the worker will learn the result. “Someone will sort it out” does not tell the next shift what is unresolved. In a formal refusal, read the employer's investigation report and raise remaining concerns through the process. OHS is the external safety route; Employment Standards deals with matters such as wages and employment hours.
Optional first-step hint: “Write one observed fact, one thing still unknown and one action Devin can take from the clear doorway. Avoid naming the chemical.”

Optional supplied video — A first-shift hazard. Use the player if a narrated example helps. You may also read the written equivalent beside it. The video shows the same information gap; it is not a chemical-handling demonstration. Its pause instruction can be answered in the optional field My video pause response: observation, missing information and next safe action. Watching or using that field is not required. The Alberta process in Document C supplies the specific refusal threshold.

I begin with Devin's actual position: the work has not started, and Jo is reachable from a clear doorway. That makes it possible to pause and report without handling the container. I do not invent a spill because a general safety illustration happens to show one.

My observation is the unreadable label and missing training. My information request follows from those gaps: product identity, hazard information, approved procedure and appropriate instruction. “Give me any gloves” would jump to equipment before anyone has identified what the equipment needs to protect against.
Here is Devin's complete report and follow-up plan:

This uses the right to know and participate immediately. It also identifies the refusal route without pretending a classroom paragraph has already made a legal finding. “Use a small amount to see whether it works” is an unsafe alternative because the proposed test itself could cause exposure.

heads: A new hazard: the damaged vacuum cord
prose: Imani is a new employee in fictional Alder Display Shop, an Alberta provincially regulated workplace. Create a safe-response handoff using the following complete records. Do not perform a real inspection, repair or test.

Document D — Observation, October 9, 2026, 5:20 p.m. Imani is asked to vacuum a dry sales-floor area. The vacuum is switched off and already unplugged. Before touching it, Imani sees a split in the cord insulation with metal visible. No one has been shocked; there is no fire, smoke, water or immediate injury. Imani stands in a clear area and has not moved, plugged in or tested the machine. Supervisor Ren is at the nearby service desk and can be reached safely.

Document E — Training and instructions. Imani has ordinary vacuum-use instruction, but no electrical repair training or authority to repair equipment. The shop's written procedure says: “Do not use damaged electrical equipment. Report the equipment and location to Ren; Ren arranges removal from service and assessment by a competent person. Workers must not improvise repairs. A replacement may be used only after its condition and safe use are confirmed.” A coworker says, “Wrap it in tape and finish quickly.” No replacement has yet been supplied.

Success means a specific report, no testing or improvised repair, appropriate responsibility for controls, and a follow-up that does not silently pass damaged equipment to another worker. You may describe a safe replacement or another safe task; do not assume either has already been supplied.

title: Act on responsibilities and concerns

heads: What a useful concern report needs to establish
Separate a report from a confirmed resolution
Make the evidence and route traceable
prose: A concern report should help someone who was not present understand the event, the response already taken and what remains unresolved. Learn to keep those parts separate before reading the timeline.

Documentation is a record preserving relevant facts and actions. An observation states what was seen or heard. A request states what response is needed. An acknowledgement confirms that a message was received; it does not establish that a hazard was corrected or a payment fixed.

For a simple example, “The worker reported the missing guard at 10:00; the supervisor received the message at 10:10” records a report and receipt. It does not confirm inspection, repair or permission to use the equipment. Record those outcomes only when evidence supplies them.

Use who, date and time, location or record, observed fact, action already taken and requested response. Distinguish an exact supplied quotation from a summary and your observation from another person’s statement. Avoid guessing a person’s intention.

A pay concern needs the same pay period and kind of amount on both records. Gross regular earnings are hours multiplied by the supplied rate; net pay is after deductions. A different net deposit alone does not establish a missing regular-hours payment.

Choose a route suited to the concern: workplace safety, wages and protected-ground treatment involve different responsibilities and official processes. The supplied source records explain the relevant steps. Preserve original records and add dated corrections rather than changing originals to make them agree.

When you read the case: Read the chronology for what is confirmed at each time. The first check asks about the status of the concern at a particular point. Keep “reported,” “received,” “being checked” and “resolved” distinct while writing your later response.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

A concern becomes easier to act on when another person can understand what happened, locate the evidence and see what response is needed. “Work was unfair” may describe a feeling accurately, but a report also needs the event, date, records and requested action.

You will follow a report about a missing machine guard, practise recording a response without declaring the issue resolved too soon, then investigate a different worker's pay-record discrepancy. Your final product will be a factual review request with a calculation and a suitable follow-up route.

Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Use the method with the case → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. You can pause after the example or before the new case. Everything needed is supplied. Writing saves automatically; practice answers and model comparisons do not grade you. The independent report and review sign-offs become your lesson evidence.

Vocabulary. An observation records what someone saw, heard or did. An inference is an interpretation drawn from information. A discrepancy is a difference between records that should agree. A pay period is the date range covered by a pay statement. Gross regular wages are earnings for regular hours before deductions; net pay is what remains after deductions. A follow-up records what happened after the first report. Advocacy means expressing a need or right and requesting action supported by evidence.

Optional disclosure: Official sources for real questions. The dated source records are available within the lesson. Current links are optional; this activity does not submit an actual complaint or require contact with a workplace.

heads: Document A — Owen's observation note, October 7, 2026
Document B — Training card and report log
Document C — In-course responsibilities and source map
Read the documents
prose: Owen is an employee at fictional Birch Sign Workshop in Alberta, a provincially regulated workplace. Owen has been trained to use Cutter 2 only with its fitted safety guard in place. Owen has not been trained to repair or alter the equipment.

Training card: “Before use, verify the fitted guard is present. If it is absent or damaged, do not operate Cutter 2. Report to Tessa. Only an authorized competent person may inspect, repair and clear the machine for use. Do not perform a test cut to check an unguarded machine.”
Report log, October 7:
These facts establish an observation, a report and an interim response. They do not establish who removed the guard or that the machine has been cleared for use.
Government of Alberta records, checked September 28, 2026:
The selected source depends on the question. You may need more than one route if a situation contains different issues. None of these services is an all-purpose “workplace complaint department.”
tables: Time Recorded event 4:08 p.m. Owen told Tessa that Cutter 2's guard was missing and the task had not started. 4:10 p.m. Tessa said, “Keep it out of use. I will arrange a competent inspection. Work at the packing table, which you are trained to use.” 4:15 p.m. Owen began the safe packing task. No inspection result had yet been provided.

Topic and source Limited paraphrase relevant here Young worker rights and responsibilities — “Workplace safety,” “Job training” Workers report unsafe conditions, follow safe procedures and ask for needed training. Employers ensure workers have the training and skills to do their work safely. Employer responsibilities — “Overview” Employers arrange competent supervision, hazard information, safe practices and required safety training/equipment. A worker's report does not transfer the employer's responsibility to provide controls to that worker. Refuse dangerous work — “Worker obligations,” “Employer obligations” Dangerous-work refusals require prompt notice and employer investigation. Unless resolved immediately, the worker receives the investigation report. Safe alternative work may be assigned. Unresolved danger belongs with Occupational Health and Safety (OHS). Payment of earnings — “Pay statements” Statements identify the pay period, work hours and rates, separate earnings items and deductions with their reasons. This makes comparison with an employee's records possible. Make an employment standards complaint — “What a complaint can be about,” “Other workplace issues not covered” Provincial Employment Standards handles matters such as wages and hours. Safety concerns go to OHS; protected-ground discrimination concerns go to the Alberta Human Rights Commission. Eligibility and procedures differ.

heads: Make the concern traceable
Explain the responsibility without guessing intent
Read records on the same basis
Select the route that can address the issue
Recognize other employment-standards questions
Preserve the evidence and the outcome
prose: A report needs enough detail for someone who was not present. Include who, when, where, what was observed, what was done, and what response is requested. Use a date as well as a clock time; “yesterday” becomes unclear when the note is read next week. Name the machine or pay period so the recipient does not check the wrong record.

Record the source of information. “I saw the guard was absent” differs from “a coworker said the guard had been repaired.” The first is Owen's observation; the second would be another person's statement. Both could be relevant, but they are different forms of evidence. Quote only words supplied as exact words. If you remember the meaning rather than the wording in a real situation, label it as a summary.

Owen's responsibilities are to avoid the prohibited use, report the condition and follow safe arrangements. The employer's responsibilities include ensuring safe practices, competent assessment and training. Owen can name those responsibilities without saying “Tessa deliberately endangered me.” A report about the condition is useful even when the reason for it is unknown.

Use a clear request: “Please confirm the inspection outcome and the conditions for resuming use.” This is more actionable than “make the workplace better.” An initial response can be useful without being the final resolution: moving Owen to packing reduces immediate exposure but does not repair or clear Cutter 2.

For a wages question, first compare the same dates and kind of amount. A four-hour personal work record cannot be compared directly with a whole month's net deposit. Find the matching pay period and the regular-hours line. Then compare hours × rate with gross regular wages. Deductions affect net pay; they do not explain why a statement's regular-hours line differs from the work record.

For example, a clearly labelled fictional illustration of two regular hours at $20 per hour produces $40 of regular wages before deductions. A $37 net deposit could reflect deductions and does not by itself prove three dollars of unpaid regular wages. You would need the earnings and deduction lines. In the independent case, the necessary lines and timing are supplied; do not invent tax rates.

An internal request and a formal complaint are different actions. The Employment Standards source explains starting with the employer and, for ordinary pay issues, waiting one pay period before a formal complaint to see whether the next statement resolves it. Urgent matters can differ. Its question service can help explain the applicable process; asking a question is not filing a complaint. A record should not promise an agency will accept a complaint or decide in the worker's favour.

Pay concerns can involve more than the regular hours shown on a statement. Dated source record — checked September 28, 2026: Alberta's Employment Standards rules cover the categories below. Recognizing the category helps identify the right records and official explanation before deciding what is owed.

The optional official rules directory links to each category. This overview gives no new legal rates or entitlement calculation. The later regular-wage case supplies the information needed for its stated comparison; do not add hypothetical holiday, overtime, vacation or termination amounts to it. Safety hazards still belong with the OHS route, and possible discrimination with the human-rights route.

Keep a copy of the relevant original record and the dated response. Do not alter an original time entry just to make it match payroll. If you find your own error, write a dated correction that preserves what changed. Record resolution with specifics: what was corrected, by whom and how you know. “Closed” with no evidence prevents later checking.
Optional first-step hint: “Turn 'the machine is dangerous' into an observation with a date, machine name and missing part. Then add the action already taken and the response still needed.”
tables: Evidence you are investigating Suitable first organizational recipient Relevant outside information route Missing guard or unresolved danger Supervisor/employer or designated safety contact Alberta OHS Hours or regular-wage discrepancy Payroll/employer with the dated records Alberta Employment Standards Negative treatment possibly connected to a protected ground Appropriate support/HR contact when safe and useful Alberta Human Rights Commission

Category What it concerns and what to verify in a real case Vacation time and vacation pay Time away from work and the pay connected with vacation are related but distinct. Check length of employment, applicable eligibility, time taken and vacation pay already recorded or paid. A vacation-pay entry alone does not describe when time off was taken. General holidays Rules for recognized holidays and associated pay or time off. Check the holiday, eligibility, whether it was a regular workday and whether the employee worked. Do not assume every holiday or worker has the same arrangement. Overtime Work hours that meet applicable overtime rules, and the resulting compensation or a valid arrangement for paid time off. Check daily and weekly time records, applicable occupation or industry exceptions and any written agreement. A long shift by itself does not settle the calculation. Ending employment Questions about notice, possible termination pay and final earnings when an employment relationship ends. Check who ended it, length of employment, the circumstances and applicable exceptions. A temporary lay-off and a permanent end of employment are different situations.

prose: I start the report at 4:05, before the later conversation, so the sequence is clear. The missing guard is the observed condition. The training card explains why it matters: Owen must not use Cutter 2 without it. I can state that connection without claiming an injury or knowing who removed the guard.

Next I record both sides of the response. Owen reported at 4:08 and Tessa acted at 4:10. Omitting Tessa's actual response would make the record misleading. Finally I say what remains open: a competent inspection and clearance. Safe packing work does not establish that Cutter 2 is safe.
Complete report, prepared at 4:20 p.m. on October 7:

“Tessa did nothing and the machine was fine by 4:15” contradicts the documents twice. It ignores the interim instruction and invents a final outcome. Reliable advocacy depends on describing both the concern and any action already taken.

title: Read a pay stub

heads: Understand the parts of a pay stub
Follow gross pay, deductions and net pay
Match the period before comparing records
prose: A pay stub is an employer’s written breakdown of a payment for work. Before reading one, learn which work period it covers and how earnings become the amount paid.

Gross pay is earnings before deductions. For regular hourly work, use the supplied hours × hourly rate. A deduction is an amount removed from gross pay. Net pay is the amount remaining after the listed deductions.

In a small invented example, three hours at $18 produces $54 gross earnings. If the statement lists $6 of deductions, net pay is $48. These are supplied practice amounts, not tax or contribution rates. Deductions have already been removed from net pay; subtracting them again would count them twice.

A pay period identifies the work included. The payment date says when the money is paid. Current means this period; year to date combines payments in the calendar year. Current gross and year-to-date deductions belong to different comparisons.

Use matching time entries → current hours and rate → current gross → current deductions → current net → deposit. A deposit matching the net box does not prove the hours are correct. Read the pay-period dates on the stub and time record before checking the amounts.
If two records disagree, state the specific line and difference. The mismatch does not by itself tell you whether the cause was recording, approval or processing.

When you read the case: Begin by locating the pay period and the current-hours line. The first reading check asks which records to compare to check the hours for this payment. Later you will calculate the supplied gross, deductions and net.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Did the payment match the work?
prose: Mika has received a pay stub: the employer's written breakdown of a payment for work. The amount deposited is smaller than hours multiplied by the hourly wage. That difference might be an explained deduction, an error, or a detail that needs checking. Looking only at the deposit cannot tell you which.

You will learn to follow the payment from hours to earnings to deductions to the amount received. Your final product is a short pay-check note for a different worker, including calculations and a question about a mismatch. All records are fictional. You will not enter your own employment or tax information.
How to complete this lesson

You can pause after the guided calculation. All entries save; practice is separate from the final note. Optional Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) reference and vocabulary disclosures sit beside this roadmap.

heads: Read Mika's records
prose: Mika is an adult working at the fictional Pine Street Print Shop. A time record lists hours worked. A pay stub explains how an employer calculated a payment. A bank deposit is evidence of money received, but does not show the whole calculation. Read the two documents together.
Pine Street Print Shop — statement of earnings

Employee: Mika. Pay period: September 1–14, 2026. Payment date: September 18, 2026. Currency: Canadian dollars. This exercise includes one regular-pay line and three supplied deductions; no overtime, vacation-pay line, reimbursements or other adjustments.
Payment summary: current gross $225.00; current deductions $30.40; current net deposit $194.60. Year-to-date net: $973.00.

Mika's time record: September 3, 4.00 hours; September 7, 4.50 hours; September 12, 4.00 hours. Mika confirms these are the hours actually worked. All deduction amounts are fictional supplied figures for reading practice, not rates or eligibility rules to use for a real worker.

prose: Gross pay is earnings before deductions. For the single regular-pay line in this case, multiply hours by the hourly rate. The unit check helps: hours × dollars per hour produces dollars. The decimal 12.50 means twelve and a half hours; it does not mean twelve hours and fifty minutes.

A deduction is an amount removed from gross pay. Some payroll deductions contribute to public programs or tax withholding; others can relate to benefits or an agreed arrangement. The label tells you what is being withheld. It does not by itself prove the amount is correct or that it applies to every worker. In this lesson the amounts are supplied, so add them. Do not try to calculate current tax or contribution rates from memory.

Net pay is what remains after the listed deductions. It is the amount this statement says should be paid. Subtract deductions once: they are already removed from the displayed net amount. If you begin a spending plan with net pay and subtract them again, you make the available payment too small.

One-payment map: time entries → hours × rate → gross earnings → subtract current deductions → net payment. A second check compares that net figure with the actual deposit. A matching deposit can still come from incorrect hours, which is why checking only the last box is insufficient.

A different stub may include several earnings lines. Overtime is pay recorded for hours treated as overtime under the applicable arrangement; an additional earning might be a separately listed bonus. Read each line's supplied hours, rate and amount before adding gross pay. Do not assume that every worker's overtime threshold or rate is the same.

A second format to read: a fictional adult worker's statement lists regular earnings, 10 hours at $20 = $200; approved overtime earnings, 2 hours at the expressly supplied $30 rate = $60; and a $15 bonus. Gross is $200 + $60 + $15 = $275. These are the statement's supplied terms, not a lesson about legal overtime eligibility. A separately labelled expense reimbursement is money repaid for an expense; inspect its treatment on the actual statement instead of automatically calling every deposit amount wages.

Current means this pay period. Year to date combines payments within the current calendar year. The figures serve different questions. Use current amounts to check this deposit; use the cumulative column to examine totals over the year. Never subtract cumulative deductions from one period's gross.

The pay period and payment date also answer different questions. The period tells you which work is included. The payment date tells you when the money is paid. A shift after September 14 would not automatically belong on this stub simply because payment arrived September 18.

If the time record and stub disagree, identify the two records, period and difference. An omitted shift is a possible explanation, but the documents may not tell you whether the cause was entry, approval or processing. A useful question requests a check of a specific line. “You stole my pay” is an unsupported conclusion from a mismatch alone.

CRA reading note — retrieved September 28, 2026: the CRA's pay-stub lesson distinguishes the pay period, current amounts and year-to-date totals. Use those labels to keep your calculation within one payment. Optional CRA explanation.

heads: Check Mika's payment
prose: I start with the dates: all three time entries fall inside September 1–14. Their hours total 4.00 + 4.50 + 4.00 = 12.50 hours. That matches the regular-work line. I multiply 12.50 × $18.00 = $225.00 gross.

Next I add only the current deductions: $16.00 + $10.80 + $3.60 = $30.40. Subtracting gives $225.00 − $30.40 = $194.60 net. The payment summary reports that amount. I can therefore say the supplied arithmetic and time entries agree; I have not independently verified real payroll rules.

Completed pay-check note: “For September 1–14, Mika recorded 12.50 hours. At $18.00 per hour, gross pay is $225.00. Current deductions total $30.40, leaving $194.60. These figures match the supplied statement. The record supports this calculation; it does not establish that the fictional deductions would apply to another worker.”

An answer of $73.00 comes from $225.00 − $152.00. It uses the year-to-date deduction total. The subtraction is arithmetically possible, but its two numbers describe different spans of time. Choosing the appropriate figures is part of doing the calculation correctly.
