title: What shapes a money decision?

heads: Work out what is available before weighing a purchase
Separate money held from money available
Recognize influences without letting them do the arithmetic
prose: A money decision has an amount, a purpose and influences around it. Before reading the purchase situation, learn to protect existing commitments and recognize what may be pushing the choice.
A commitment is money already needed for a planned obligation. A constraint is a limit the choice must respect. The money visible in an account is not necessarily all available for a new purchase.

For a simple example, someone has $50, with $20 needed for travel and $10 for supplies. Available for a new choice is $50 − $20 − $10 = $20. A $30 item can be paid for physically, but buying it would leave too little for those commitments.

A need is a requirement in the situation; a want is a desire without the same immediate necessity. Identify the function needed. A usable bag and a particular brand of bag do not necessarily serve different essential functions.

A contextual influence comes from circumstances or relationships, such as transport options or group plans. A psychological influence comes from feelings, thoughts or habits. A marketing influence comes from how an offer is presented, such as a deadline or highlighted price.

These can overlap. Wanting to belong and seeing a limited-time offer can make a purchase feel urgent; they do not increase the available amount. Use commitments → money left → benefit sought → pressure or assumption → feasible choice and consequence. A choice should explain what is protected and what is postponed.

When you read the case: Read the money note for the existing commitments before interpreting the advertisement. The first check asks what remains after those amounts. Later you will explain the influences and a choice that fits the supplied situation.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: A purchase can fit the price tag and still squeeze the plan
prose: Ari wants the hoodie friends are ordering. There is enough money to pay its price today, but some of that money already has a job. You will work out what is available, then consider why the choice feels urgent.

Your final product is a decision note for Ren: explain a purchase choice using the supplied budget, a personal priority and an influence worth questioning. You are not expected to disclose your family's finances or agree with someone else's spending values.

How to complete this lesson: Read Ari's next two weeks and check the money already committed. Work through Separate the amount from the pressure and its complete decision example. Try Change one fact, answer six understanding questions, then write Ren's backpack decision. Compare, revise and sign off. Pause after the practice if useful; entries save automatically. Practice checks support revision; the Ren note is final evidence.

heads: Ari's next two weeks
prose: Ari is a fictional student with $60 available now. No more money arrives during the next fourteen days. Necessary meals and housing are provided separately and do not come out of this $60. Ari has two commitments before the next payment: $42 for transit to school and $12 to repair the zipper on the bag used daily. There is no usable spare bag. Both commitments must be paid within the fourteen days.
The group order notice
“Club hoodie: $48, including all charges. Orders close tonight. The club's regular activities are open to members with or without a hoodie. No returns after a personalized order is placed.”
Three messages Ari sees
Ari likes belonging to the club and likes colourful clothing. Ari also wants reliable travel to school. Those are real priorities in the case; neither needs to be mocked to examine the purchase.

heads: Separate the amount from the pressure
Notice three kinds of influence
Respect values and examine the claim
prose: A commitment is money already needed for a planned obligation. Available for this choice means what remains after those commitments, not the whole amount in an account. Ari can physically pay $48 now, but doing so would leave $12 for $54 of commitments. The consequence is a shortfall, not simply a lower balance.

A need is a requirement in the person's situation; a want is something desired without the same immediate necessity. Context matters. A bag can be necessary for carrying supplies, while a particular brand may be optional. It is more useful to identify the job an item must do than to label every version of the item a need. Ari needs usable storage and travel; the case says the hoodie is not needed to join club activities.

A contextual influence comes from circumstances and relationships: travel options, family habits, cultural practices, community expectations or advice. A psychological influence involves how a person feels, thinks or habitually acts: excitement, anxiety about missing out, buying when stressed or assuming a higher price means higher quality. A marketing influence is part of how an offer is presented, such as a countdown or a small weekly price.

These can overlap. Ari's wish to belong is a feeling, the group photo is a social situation, and the deadline is part of the selling message. The deadline may be accurate, but it does not make extra money appear. Ask two separate questions: “Is the deadline real?” and “Does this purchase fit the commitments?” A truthful advertisement can still emphasize the part of a decision that makes buying feel attractive.

A value is something a person considers important. Someone may value shared celebrations, independence, generosity or avoiding debt. Families and communities can hold different views, and individuals within them can disagree. Do not infer a person's beliefs from their background. Use the priorities actually supplied.

A belief such as “using credit always means you can afford something” can be tested: borrowing moves a payment into the future and may add costs. A different belief, “borrowing is always a personal failure,” also overlooks context, such as a planned education expense with a feasible repayment plan. In this lesson there is no borrowing offer or future income available to solve Ari's gap. Inventing one would avoid the decision the records actually support.

Decision path: commitments → money left → benefit sought → pressure or assumption → feasible choice and consequence. A feasible choice fits the supplied money and deadlines. The explanation should show which benefit is kept and which is postponed.

In-course FCAC note, read September 28, 2026: needs and wants depend on a person's circumstances. Identify the function Ari must protect before judging the item. Read “Evaluate your needs and wants” — Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (new tab) ↗.

heads: Explain Ari's choice without judging Ari
prose: I first reserve $42 + $12 = $54. That leaves $6. The hoodie costs $48, so buying it from the remaining money would require another $42. Ari does not have that extra money in the case.

The club notice matters as much as the numbers. It says regular participation does not require the hoodie. Ari can keep the belonging benefit of attending club activities while giving up the matching clothing. The group photo and countdown explain why waiting feels uncomfortable; neither changes the available $6.

Completed decision note: “I recommend Ari skip this order and protect the $54 for transit and the bag repair. Only $6 is uncommitted, so the $48 hoodie would leave a $42 gap. Ari values belonging, but the notice says the club remains open without the hoodie. The group photo and closing deadline create pressure to buy now. Ari could attend in existing clothing and plan for a later optional purchase when money is available.”
“Only careless people buy club clothing” is not supported. The problem is this budget and timing. With different resources, buying the same hoodie could be a reasonable choice.

title: Build a flexible budget

heads: A budget must fit both the total and the calendar
Learn the budget and cash-flow terms
Carry the balance through the dates
prose: A monthly total can look affordable while a bill arrives before the money needed to pay it. This lesson teaches two checks: the whole-period plan and the money available on each date.

A budget plans income, spending and money set aside. A cash-flow calendar puts money received and paid in date order. The opening balance is the money available at the start; a running balance is the amount after each movement.

Income minus expenses and planned saving gives a surplus if positive or a shortfall if negative. That whole-period result does not establish that every bill can be paid on time. Money due later is not available earlier.

For a small invented example, start with $30. Pay a $20 bill on Wednesday: $10 remains. Receive $40 on Friday: $50 is then available. The Friday payment does not change what was available on Wednesday.

Use opening balance + income received − payments made = balance at this point. Carry that result into the next date. Identify the lowest balance, as well as the final one. In the lesson’s model, a negative balance signals using money not available; no overdraft terms are supplied.

A buffer is accessible money reserved for variation. A changed payment date works only when the case confirms the arrangement. Removing a necessary expense or assuming an unapproved extension hides the problem rather than establishing a workable plan.

When you read the case: Read the opening money, income dates and bill dates together. The first reading check concerns money available on one date. Later you will test the full total and calendar and explain a confirmed adjustment.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Will the money be there on the day it is needed?
prose: Sam's planned monthly spending is lower than monthly income. That sounds reassuring, until several bills arrive before the second payment. A budget needs both totals and dates.

You will read a money calendar, find its lowest balance and revise a plan using confirmed options. Your final product is a dated plan for Nico that covers the stated commitments without spending money before it arrives. All budgets are fictional and all amounts are Canadian dollars. A calculator is available; the challenge is deciding what belongs in the calculation.

Income is available before any outgoing payment on the same date. The $80 is an opening balance, not another monthly wage. No overdraft, credit or other income is available in this case.
Planned payments

Housing and food amounts are exercise assumptions, not suggested living-cost estimates. Sam wants to finish the month with at least the original $80 account buffer. Transfers to savings move money out of this spending account but do not destroy it; keep them in the cash-flow calculation because that money is no longer available here.

heads: Two checks for a workable budget
Separate a feasible change from a wish
prose: A budget is a plan for receiving, using and setting aside money. A cash-flow calendar puts those movements in date order. Start with the opening balance, add money when it arrives and subtract payments when they leave. The number after each movement is a running balance.

First check the whole period: income minus expenses and planned saving. A positive result is a surplus; a negative result is a shortfall. A surplus does not mean that every day is covered. If the second payment arrives after a bill, that later income cannot pay the earlier bill without some arrangement that actually makes money available.

Second check timing: calculate the running balance through the month. The lowest balance is the smallest amount reached after a movement. In this case any negative amount signals that the plan uses money unavailable in the account. It is a planning warning, not a fee calculation. No overdraft terms have been supplied.

Calendar method: opening balance + income received − payments made = balance at this point. Repeat from the new balance, not from zero. A simple sequence of dated balances makes a timing problem visible even when the monthly total looks fine.

Some amounts are fixed by the case; others can change. Food and transit are required here. Removing them produces a lower total while leaving Sam unable to carry out the stated plan. A confirmed payment arrangement can change a date without changing total cost. A request that has not been accepted cannot be treated as an agreement.

Overextending means committing more money than the plan can support, including repayments that leave too little for other obligations. A small individual payment can contribute to overextension when several commitments fall together. Check their combined effects rather than judging one price in isolation.

A buffer is money left accessible for variation. It has a job even while unspent. However, a buffer target can sometimes need review: preserving it at all costs is not more important than a real essential need. State the trade-off rather than pretending there is no constraint.

Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) reading note, September 28, 2026: its budgeting guidance connects income, spending and saving, and recommends reviewing the plan as circumstances change. Here, the dated records let you perform that review inside the lesson. Optional “Making a budget”.

heads: Repair Sam's timing problem
prose: The planned payments total $420 + $90 + $45 + $80 + $90 + $60 + $70 + $35 = $890. Income totals $900, so the month adds $10 to the original $80. Ending with $90 looks possible on totals alone.

Now I follow the dates. After the first income, Sam has $530. Room payment leaves $110; food leaves $20; phone takes the plan to −$25; transit takes it to −$105. The second income comes too late to prevent those shortfalls. I have found the problem before guessing at a solution.
The room agreement already supplies a permitted alternative. Splitting that payment produces this completed calendar:

The account stays nonnegative. The lowest balance during the month after the first payment arrives is $90; including the starting point, the minimum is the opening $80. The important pre-payday balance is $105. State which interval you mean when reporting a minimum.

Completed recommendation: “Use the confirmed $210/$210 room arrangement. It leaves $105 just before the October 15 income, covers all listed payments and ends at $90. Total monthly spending and saving remain $890. I changed timing using an available agreement, not the amount of income.”
“Just pay the phone late” is unsupported: no extension is supplied. The split-room option is defensible because its dates and no-fee permission are written in the case.

title: Compare a major purchase

heads: Compare an agreement’s total and its first payment
Read the payment and ownership terms
Compare the same period and what protection covers
prose: A major purchase can be paid for in several ways. A small monthly figure does not tell you the total cost, when money is needed or what ownership and protection the agreement supplies.

An upfront cost is paid at the beginning. An instalment is one payment in a series. A recurring cost repeats. The agreement’s term describes its stated period. A lease or rental provides use under its conditions and does not automatically give ownership.

For a small invented example with no other charges, $25 at pickup plus six payments of $15 totals $115. The first-date cash requirement and the whole-period total are different questions. Count a separately stated mandatory charge once and say whether taxes are included in the supplied amount.

Use upfront amount + payment count × payment amount + additional mandatory charges = scheduled total. Compare offers over the same stated period. Keep possible future costs separate from confirmed scheduled costs.

A warranty or cover plan promises a remedy only under its terms. An exclusion identifies what is outside the cover; a claim fee can still be payable when a repair is eligible. “Covered” does not necessarily mean every future repair is free.

After calculating, check whether the payments fit the available money on their dates, what is owned at the end and which costs remain uncertain. A lower total can still require an upfront payment the person cannot meet.

When you read the case: Read each offer for the amount due initially, number of payments and what each includes. The first check asks for the scheduled-total calculation. Later you will connect the payment comparison with ownership, cover limits and the supplied budget.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Compare the whole arrangement
prose: A small monthly price can make two offers look similar. The total, commitment, ownership and costs after purchase can still differ. You will help Dani compare two laptop purchase agreements, then make an independent recommendation about a calculator rental or purchase.

Your final product is a comparison note that distinguishes total cost from cash needed now, explains what the user receives and identifies one fact still worth checking. All offers are invented and all prices include the charges specified in the case. No purchase or live shopping is required.

How to complete this lesson: Read Dani's laptop offers and locate the payment terms. Learn Put offers on the same basis, then follow the complete comparison. In Add a repair possibility, test how one event changes the totals. Answer six questions and complete Riley's sixteen-week calculator choice. Review the model, revise and sign off. Pause after the laptop comparison if needed; every field saves.

heads: Dani's laptop offers
prose: Dani needs a laptop for a two-year program starting next month. Both offers supply the same model, which the fictional program has confirmed meets its software requirements. Dani has $120 available now and can commit up to $40 each month for 24 months after other obligations. Dani has no other purchase fund or borrowing option in this case.
North Computer Shop — purchase offer A

Pay $120 at pickup and $34 each month for 24 months. All scheduled charges and taxes are included. Ownership transfers after the final payment. The price includes a one-year warranty for manufacturing defects, not accidental damage. Accidental repair costs are not supplied. Cancelling does not erase the unpaid purchase balance. There is no extra fee for paying the balance early.
Central Computer Shop — purchase offer B

Pay $0 at pickup and $41 each month for 24 months. All scheduled charges and taxes are included. Same ownership and early-payment terms as A. Same one-year defect warranty, plus 24 months of accidental-damage cover: one eligible repair, with a $50 claim fee. Loss and theft are excluded. No repair occurs in the base comparison.

heads: Put offers on the same basis
Compare benefits and remaining exposure
Keep ownership costs visible
prose: A purchase agreement sets out how a buyer pays for an item and what conditions apply. An instalment is one payment in a series. The term is the period covered by the agreement. A lease or rental pays for use under stated conditions and does not automatically give ownership. Read the ownership rule rather than assuming that the smallest monthly price buys the item.

Choose the same comparison period. Here both offers last 24 months. Add the upfront amount, all scheduled payments and any other mandatory charges. Do not add a fee twice if the offer already includes it. This gives a scheduled total under stated assumptions; a possible repair should be shown separately until an event is specified.

Cost map: amount at pickup + number of payments × payment amount + additional mandatory charges = scheduled total. Alongside it, keep a second line: money needed on the first date and on each later date. A lower total can still be inaccessible if the upfront payment is too large.

A warranty promises a remedy for conditions described in its terms. It is not a promise that every future problem will be free. A cover plan can have exclusions, limits and a claim fee. B includes one eligible accidental repair, but theft remains excluded and an accepted claim still costs $50. Writing “B includes free repairs” would erase important terms.

A decision should connect the feature to a plausible need. Both computers already meet the program's software requirements, so a claim that the more expensive plan runs the software better is unsupported. The useful difference is the cover, together with its price and limits.

Large purchases can create later costs: maintenance, insurance where needed, replacement parts, interest, storage or operating costs. A vehicle, for example, can require insurance and ongoing maintenance in addition to its purchase price. Amounts depend on the actual vehicle, use and agreement, so do not invent a universal estimate. Mark missing costs and find an appropriate quote before a real commitment.

In this case the task supplies enough to compare scheduled payments. It does not supply a probability of accidental damage or A's repair prices. You can identify exposure without pretending to calculate an expected repair bill.

Optional reference note, September 28, 2026: The personal-loan comparison method from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) checks payment count and total repayment, alongside fees. Here that arithmetic helps compare the supplied agreements; it does not establish a real loan's legal terms. Read “Comparing loan options”.

heads: Compare Dani's base plan
prose: Offer A totals $120 + 24 × $34 = $936. Offer B totals 24 × $41 = $984. B costs $48 more in scheduled payments. That difference buys a defined cover feature, not a different computer.

Now I check Dani's resources. A needs the full $120 available at pickup and then $34 monthly, leaving $6 of the $40 monthly allowance. B needs no upfront payment but requires $41 each month, $1 above the stated limit. Having no upfront payment does not solve that repeated shortfall.

Completed comparison: “Offer A fits Dani's supplied upfront and monthly limits and has a $936 scheduled total. B costs $984 and includes one eligible accidental repair with a $50 claim fee, but its $41 monthly payment exceeds Dani's $40 limit. I recommend A within this case, while checking repair prices before a real purchase and considering how to set aside the remaining $6 monthly. A's warranty does not cover accidental damage; the cheaper scheduled total does not eliminate repair risk.”

The alternative “B is best because it costs nothing today” considers only the first date. The alternative “A will definitely cost less under every possible event” confuses a base comparison with a guarantee about unknown repairs.

title: Read a borrowing offer

heads: Know what a borrowing offer’s numbers represent
Separate principal, charges and repayment
Read the complete schedule
prose: A borrowing offer contains money received now and obligations paid later. Learn to distinguish those amounts before comparing the offers.

Credit is an arrangement permitting borrowing. Debt is the amount owed. Principal is the amount borrowed before interest and other charges. Interest is a borrowing charge; a fee is another specified charge.

A payment is an amount due at a scheduled time. Total repayment includes returning the principal. Cost of borrowing is the amount paid above the principal, including the relevant fees in the comparison. Those measures answer different questions.

For a small invented offer, receive $100, make six payments of $20 and pay a separate $5 fee. Total paid is $125; the amount above the $100 principal is $25. A $20 payment is neither the amount borrowed nor the full borrowing cost.

An instalment loan uses a stated payment series. A line of credit permits borrowing up to a limit under its terms; the amount actually borrowed may change. A limit is permission to borrow, not income. Read each product’s payment and access rules.

Use amount received → payment frequency and count → fees → total paid → amount above principal → fit with available repayment money. A longer series can produce a smaller payment while costing more overall.

When you read the case: Identify which offer figure is a payment, principal, fee or total. The first check asks what one advertised payment describes. The later comparison asks you to calculate totals and explain whether the obligation fits the supplied budget.

Your final product is a borrowing decision for a different fictional adult, including a non-borrowing alternative. You will not apply for credit, supply identification or enter real financial details.

heads: Alex's two offer summaries
prose: Alex is a fictional adult considering borrowing $600 for equipment needed next month. After all other commitments, Alex has $60 each month available for repayment and $20 separately available now for a setup fee. Both offers provide exactly $600; no optional insurance is included. All required payments are stated, and neither offer permits additional borrowing through the same agreement.
Offer A — fixed instalment loan

Receive $600. Repay $55 monthly for twelve months, starting one month after receiving the money. No setup fee or other charge if paid as scheduled. The payment total includes the loan principal and borrowing charges. Missed-payment consequences and early-payment terms are not supplied; they need checking before a real agreement.
Offer B — longer instalment loan

Receive $600. Pay a separate $15 setup fee from existing cash when the loan begins. Repay $31 monthly for twenty-four months, starting one month later. The payments include principal and borrowing charges; the separate setup fee is not included in the $31. No other charge if paid as scheduled. Missed-payment and early-payment terms remain unspecified.
Application-information card

A lender may examine identity, income, existing obligations and credit history before approving an application. A quote is not approval. Some products require collateral or another responsible borrower. You are reading a fictional offer, not deciding legal eligibility or completing an application.

heads: Separate the money borrowed from the promise to repay
Recognize purposes and responsibilities
Test the commitment, not just approval
prose: Credit is an arrangement that permits borrowing. Debt is the amount owed after borrowing occurs. The principal is the borrowed amount before interest and other charges. Interest is a charge for using borrowed money, while a fee is another specified charge. Total repayment includes returning the principal; cost of borrowing is the amount paid above the principal, including relevant fees in the comparison.

An instalment loan provides an amount repaid through a stated series of payments. A line of credit permits borrowing up to a limit under its terms; repaid amounts may become available again, and the outstanding amount can change with new borrowing. A credit limit is not a gift or income. Paying only interest on an outstanding line-of-credit balance does not reduce the principal.

Offer-reading map: amount received → payment amount and frequency → number of payments → fees → total paid → amount above principal → fit with the repayment budget. Keep separately paid fees separate until adding the total, so they are not omitted or counted twice.

Different products serve different purposes. A vehicle loan finances a vehicle and may use that vehicle as collateral, an asset securing repayment. A mortgage is a loan used for a property purchase, with property security and further terms. A student loan supports education under its program's rules; it is different from a bank's student line of credit. A credit-card cash advance takes borrowed cash against credit, with its own fees and interest terms. Buy now, pay later spreads or defers a purchase payment and is still credit, even when presented as a checkout option.

A secured loan has specified collateral; an unsecured loan does not use a pledged asset in that way. Unsecured does not mean optional repayment. A co-borrower shares responsibility for the debt under the agreement. Asking another person to join an application is not simply asking for a reference; the responsibility must be understood.

An app can make a product convenient and can emphasize an attractive first payment. Ease of tapping “accept” is not evidence of affordability. Read the repayment schedule before treating the approval screen as a recommendation.

A lender's willingness to offer credit does not prove that repayment will leave enough for a particular person's goals and obligations. Compare the payment with available money and consider a lower-income period. If key charges or consequences are absent, name exactly what must be clarified. Do not invent a missing late fee, and do not silently treat it as zero.

Dated Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) reference notes, read September 28, 2026: its line-of-credit explanation distinguishes a borrowing limit from money actually borrowed. Its buy-now-pay-later page identifies these arrangements as credit and directs attention to payment schedules and fees. Use these definitions to recognize the product before comparing it. Lines of credit · Buy now, pay later plans.

title: Calculate interest with the right time unit

heads: Use the same time unit as the interest rate
Read the formula’s quantities
Calculate the charge before the repayment
prose: An interest rate needs an amount and a period before it gives a charge. This lesson uses a simple-interest model with an unchanged principal and the stated months-divided-by-12 rule.

Principal, P, is the amount on which this model charges interest. The annual rate, r, must be a decimal: 6% means 6 ÷ 100 = 0.06. Time, t, must be in years when r is annual. Simple interest is I = P × r × t, without adding earlier interest to principal in this model.
Two months is 2 ÷ 12 year; six months is 0.5 year. Multiplying an annual rate by a number of months without conversion treats those months as years.
In a separate invented example, $200 at 6% annually for two months gives $200 × 0.06 × 2/12 = $2 interest. With no fees, repayment is $202. The $2 charge and $202 repayment are different amounts.

Use principal → annual rate as a decimal → time in years → interest → principal plus interest and any separately stated fee. Label the result with dollars and its period. Round using the lesson’s stated convention.

This formula is for the specified unchanged-principal model. Reducing-balance payments and interest added to a balance require different calculations. The next loan-schedule lesson shows that distinction; do not assume every loan follows this formula for its full length.

When you read the case: Read the agreement for the principal, annual rate, duration and time convention. Before the first check, convert the duration into the unit that belongs with the annual rate. The later tasks practise calculating and explaining the charge.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Twelve percent of what, and for how long?
prose: An interest rate needs a principal amount and a time period before it can tell you a cost. A 12% annual rate does not mean paying 12% of the principal every month. You will calculate a deliberately simple loan, then explain where that model stops being useful.

Your final product is a calculation note for a new fictional offer: show interest, principal plus interest, a missing fee and what can be concluded about a repayment limit. A calculator is provided. No real borrowing, rate lookup or personal financial information is needed.

heads: Mina's simple-interest agreement
prose: Mina is a fictional adult borrowing $600 for exactly three months. The agreement expressly uses 12% simple interest per year, with months counted as twelfths of a year. No interim payment is made; the full principal stays outstanding until the end. Interest is not added to principal during the period. Principal and interest are paid together at the end of month three. There is no setup fee or other charge in this example.
This is a mathematical teaching agreement, not an offer from a lender. Real products can calculate interest daily, add fees or use changing balances. Use this model only with the stated assumptions.
Terms on the agreement

heads: Match the rate to the time
Keep three amounts distinct
Change one assumption at a time
prose: Simple interest is calculated on the stated principal without adding earned or charged interest to that principal during the model period. Let P mean principal, r mean annual rate written as a decimal, and t mean time in years. Then I = P × r × t. I is the interest charge, not the whole repayment.

A percent means “per hundred.” Twelve percent becomes 12/100=0.12. Multiplying $600 by 12 rather than 0.12 would charge twelve times the principal for one year instead of twelve hundredths. Check whether the size of the answer makes sense: at 12% annually, one full year's simple interest on $600 is $72. Three months is only a quarter of that year, so the charge should be a quarter of $72.

The rate and time must use the same unit. With an annual rate, divide the number of months by 12. Three months is 0.25 year; six is 0.5 year. Do not apply the whole annual amount to every month. A useful alternative representation is annual interest ÷12 × number of months, which gives the same result under this agreement's month rule.

Principal is the amount borrowed. Interest is the charge calculated by the formula. Principal plus interest is the repayment before any additional fee. With a separate fee, add that fee once to the total paid. Do not call the whole repayment “interest,” and do not assume a missing fee is zero.
Write units beside each step. “600×0.12×3/12=18” becomes more meaningful as “$18 interest over three months.” A sentence about what the number means is part of the answer, not decoration around it.

For a fixed principal and simple annual rate, doubling the time doubles interest. Doubling the rate or principal also doubles interest when the other two stay constant. These relationships help catch errors, but they do not establish the behaviour of every loan.

If payments reduce the principal, later interest may apply to a smaller balance. If interest is added to a balance and later interest is charged on that enlarged amount, the process involves compounding. The following lesson uses a reducing-balance repayment schedule. It would be wrong to apply this unchanged-principal formula to that whole schedule without accounting for payments.

Model boundary: this agreement uses months/12, not an actual-days convention. A real offer must state its own calculation and fee terms. Optional FCAC background on loan rates and charges, read September 28, 2026. No external page is needed to solve the fictional agreement.

heads: Calculate Mina's three-month cost
prose: The agreement supplies P=$600, r=0.12 and t=3/12. First, $600×0.12=$72 for a full year at the stated simple rate. Three months is one-quarter of a year, so $72×0.25=$18 interest. Repayment is $600+$18=$618.

Completed calculation note: “The $600 remains outstanding for three months. At 12% simple annual interest, I=$600×0.12×3/12=$18. With no fees, Mina repays $618 at the end of the three months. The $18 is the borrowing charge; $600 is the return of principal.”

An answer of $216 comes from $600×0.12×3. It treats three months as three years. An answer of $72 uses a whole year. Neither matches the agreement's duration, even though the multiplication itself was carried out correctly.
Now you will change the duration rather than the person or calculation rule. Keep the unchanged assumptions visible when comparing results.

title: Read a loan payment schedule

heads: Learn what each loan-payment column means
Follow a payment through one row
Try a small example before the schedule
prose: A loan payment can do two jobs: pay the interest charged for the period and reduce the original debt. Learn that split before reading the repayment schedule or using the calculator.

An amortization schedule records regular payments and the debt remaining after them. The opening balance is unpaid principal before this period’s charge and payment. Interest charged is the period’s borrowing charge. Principal repaid is the part of the payment reducing the debt. The closing balance is what remains afterwards.

For this lesson’s monthly model: opening balance × monthly rate = interest; payment − interest = principal repaid; opening balance − principal repaid = closing balance. That closing balance becomes the next row’s opening balance.

In a separate invented row, opening debt is $200, the monthly rate is 1% and the payment is $22. Interest is $2, principal repaid is $20 and closing debt is $180. Subtracting the whole $22 from $200 would wrongly treat the interest portion as debt repayment.

The amortization period is the planned repayment length. Read the annual rate and the rule for converting it to a monthly rate before calculating. Alex’s and Ren’s supplied models divide the nominal annual rate by 12 and round money to cents.

Use the calculator to repeat a calculation you can explain: verify principal, rate, months and fee inputs, then compare payment size and total cost. A calculator result does not decide whether income or a purchase need will fit.

When you read the case: Next, read Alex’s agreement and schedule. Locate the separate payment, interest and principal columns before the first check. The later explanation follows the complete case calculation, and the Tools calculator supports the repayment-length comparison.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Where does a loan payment go?
prose: A payment can contain both an interest charge and repayment of the amount borrowed. You will follow those two parts through a schedule, then use a calculator to compare repayment lengths. A smaller monthly payment can help a monthly budget while increasing the total cost.

Your final product is a comparison of two fictional loans for the same purchase. You will identify the monthly payment, total borrowing cost and remaining balance after the first payment, then explain a choice using a supplied budget. All rates and terms are teaching examples, not available offers.

How to complete this lesson: Read Alex's repayment schedule. Learn what each column means, follow the first two payments, then change the repayment length in Try 24 months. Answer six checks. Complete Ren's equipment loan comparison, review the model and sign off. Pause after the calculator comparison if needed; your entries save. Practice and final work are separate.

One rule for the core lesson: divide the stated annual rate by 12 to get the monthly rate. For Alex, 12% ÷ 12 = 1% per month. Each month: opening balance × monthly rate = interest; payment − interest = principal repaid; opening balance − principal repaid = closing balance. Round money to cents. Ren uses the same method with 9% ÷ 12.

Checks help you learn; they are not grades. An incorrect answer gets a hint first. Revise and check again, or deliberately open a worked comparison when you need more support. Repeated clicks on an unchanged answer do not count as a new try.

heads: Alex's repayment schedule
prose: Alex, a fictional adult, borrows $1,000. The agreement charges a fixed nominal annual rate of 12%, divided by 12 for a monthly rate of 1%. Interest is charged on the opening balance each month. A payment is made at the end of every month. No further money is borrowed, no payments are missed and no fees apply. The loan is scheduled to finish in 12 months.

An amortization schedule is a row-by-row record of how regular payments reduce a debt. “Opening” means before this month's interest and payment; “closing” means after them. Money is rounded to cents at each interest posting. The last payment is adjusted to clear the remaining cents.

Schedule summary: 11 payments of $88.85 and a final payment of $88.84; total paid $1,066.19; total interest $66.19. Open All 12 payments to inspect the complete schedule. The visible rows and summary supply everything needed for the teaching.
tables: Month Opening balance Interest charged Payment Principal repaid Closing balance 1 $1,000.00 $10.00 $88.85 $78.85 $921.15 2 $921.15 $9.21 $88.85 $79.64 $841.51

heads: Follow one row from left to right
Explain the changing split
Use the tool as a model you can explain
prose: Start with the opening balance: the unpaid principal before that month's charge. Multiply it by the monthly rate to find interest. Subtract interest from the payment to find principal repaid. Finally, subtract principal repaid from the opening balance to find the closing balance. That closing balance becomes next month's opening balance.
The same process can be read as a flow:
Opening debt → calculate interest → split the payment → subtract its principal part → carry the balance forward.

For month one, 12% per year divided by 12 gives 1% per month, so $1,000 × 0.01 = $10. The $88.85 payment first covers that $10. The remaining $78.85 reduces principal. Subtracting the whole $88.85 from $1,000 would ignore the interest charge and understate the debt.

The payment stays almost constant, but the split changes. In month two, interest is charged on $921.15 rather than $1,000. The smaller balance produces $9.21 interest after rounding, so $79.64 of the same $88.85 payment can reduce principal. A constant payment does not mean a constant interest charge.

The amortization period is the planned time to repay the loan. Spreading the same debt over more months usually lowers each payment under the same rate and calculation rules. It also leaves some principal unpaid for longer, creating more interest charges. Both effects matter: a payment that cannot be sustained is not made suitable just by having a low lifetime cost.

The calculator repeats the row calculation. It does not know whether a purchase is needed, whether income will continue, or whether a real lender will approve an application. Read its principal, annual rate, months and fee inputs before trusting its answer. This lesson uses equal monthly payments, a fixed rate and end-of-month payments. Real agreements may use different timing or calculation conventions.

A fee paid separately adds to total cost. It does not become loan principal in this model. If a real fee is added to the loan, it can also attract interest; that would require a different principal input.

Optional reference: FCAC's Personal loans explains comparing loan terms and charges. Its page supports the comparison questions; Alex's agreement and the supplied schedule determine these figures. You do not need to open it to complete the task.

heads: Explain Alex's first two payments
prose: The first row begins with $1,000. Interest is $10, leaving $88.85 − $10 = $78.85 to repay principal. The debt falls to $1,000 − $78.85 = $921.15. The second row starts with that exact amount. Its interest is $921.15 × 0.01 = $9.2115, rounded to $9.21. Principal repaid is $88.85 − $9.21 = $79.64; the closing balance is $841.51.

Completed explanation: “Alex pays $88.85 in each of the first two months. The first payment reduces principal by $78.85 and the second by $79.64 because the second interest charge is smaller. The full schedule totals $1,066.19, which is $66.19 above the $1,000 borrowed. I used the schedule's adjusted final payment rather than multiplying $88.85 by 12 and ignoring the one-cent adjustment.”

“Alex owes $911.15 after month one” is unsupported: it subtracts the entire $88.85 payment from the $1,000 balance. Of that payment, $10 pays interest, so only $78.85 reduces the principal. Show the split once, then subtract only the principal portion from the debt.

title: Choose a repayment strategy you can sustain

heads: Understand minimum payments before choosing a strategy
Protect required payments first
Compare the priority and its consequences
prose: A repayment strategy decides how to direct money among debts. It must start with what each account requires and how much repayment money is actually available.

A minimum payment is the least required by the account’s current terms. Extra money is what remains after all required minimums. Choosing a priority for extra payments does not remove the other account’s minimum.

For a small invented example, $70 is available and two minimums are $20 and $30. The minimums use $50, leaving $20 extra. If only $40 were available, there would instead be a $10 shortfall; no extra-payment strategy creates missing money.

Highest-rate-first directs extra money to the debt with the higher rate while maintaining other minimums. Smallest-balance-first directs it to the smaller debt, which may help motivation by clearing an account sooner. Compare the supplied schedules for total interest and finish date rather than assuming either always changes both.
A sustainable plan can be repeated while protecting necessary commitments. An emergency reserve has a separate purpose; do not count it as both reserved and spent on debt.

Use balances and rates → required minimums → available extra → stated strategy → schedule cost and timing → ability to continue. Hoped-for gambling winnings or uncertain investment gains are not confirmed repayment money.

When you read the case: Read the statements for both minimums and the budget for the combined available amount. The first check asks how much is already committed to minimums. Only then compare where the remaining money goes.

heads: Give every repayment dollar a job
prose: When two debts compete for the same money, “pay more” is not a complete plan. You need the balances, rates, required payments and a realistic amount available. You will compare two strategies, then test an offer to borrow more in the hope of earning a return.

Your final product is a repayment instruction for a fictional adult: allocate a monthly budget, explain a priority and test whether a proposed investment could cover its new loan. No borrowing, betting or investment account is involved.

heads: Jo's two debt statements
prose: Jo is a fictional adult with $120 a month available for debt payments after essential costs and a small emergency saving allocation. Both accounts are up to date. Neither has a fee or early-repayment penalty in this exercise. No additional purchases are made.

The model posts interest monthly using annual rate/12, rounded to cents. Each required payment stays constant until that account's remaining balance plus interest is smaller. Unused payment money then moves to the other debt that month. The remaining part of the $120 budget is an extra payment. The full schedules are supplied; you do not need to derive them.

Same $120 monthly budget Highest-rate balance first Smallest balance first Months to clear both 11 11 Total interest $96.35 $108.65 Total paid $1,296.35 $1,308.65

heads: Protect the minimums, then choose a priority
A shortfall needs a different decision
Test the promise of a shortcut
prose: A minimum payment is the least required under that account's current terms. Choosing a priority for extra money does not give permission to skip another required payment. Jo first sets aside $70, leaving $50 to direct deliberately.

With highest-rate-first repayment, extra money goes to the debt with the higher interest rate while the other minimum continues. Each dollar of that balance removed avoids a relatively larger future charge under these fixed-rate assumptions. With smallest-balance-first repayment, extra money goes to the smaller debt. Clearing an account sooner may help someone stick to a plan, even if this costs more interest. Compare the actual schedules rather than assuming one strategy always changes the payoff month.

For Jo, both finish in 11 months, but highest-rate-first costs $12.30 less interest. This is a mathematical comparison under the supplied terms, not a judgement about Jo's character. Motivation, irregular income and past-due accounts can change practical priorities. A plan should be both affordable and repeatable.

If available money is below required payments, choosing where to put “extra” money cannot fix the shortfall. Identify the gap. Review the budget and, in a real situation, seek the creditor's current options before assuming an extension or changed terms. Do not invent income or promise to miss essential costs. A lump-sum payment can reduce debt if it is genuinely available; spending the same emergency reserve twice cannot.

An emergency fund is accessible money set aside for unexpected costs. Its purpose is to reduce the need for new borrowing after a shock. An affordable contribution and a debt plan may coexist. The amount depends on circumstances; this lesson supplies Jo's available repayment money after that allocation.

Leverage means borrowing to buy an investment. The investment may rise or fall; the debt remains payable under its agreement. If someone borrows $500 and must repay $540, an investment worth $600 at sale leaves $60 after repayment. If it is worth $450, selling it leaves a $90 shortfall. These are two invented outcomes, not forecasts. Borrowing increases exposure and adds a fixed obligation to an uncertain return.

Gambling, lotteries and sports betting also cannot supply dependable repayment income. The possible prize is not money already available. For example, four fictional $5 losing tickets cost $20 and produce no repayment money. A winning story does not establish how often winning happens or cover losses. Do not insert hoped-for winnings into a budget as though they were confirmed earnings.

Optional reading record: FCAC's Paying back your debt describes maintaining minimums while selecting a repayment priority. OSC Investor Office's What are ways to borrow money for investing? explains that investment losses do not cancel the borrowing obligation. Read September 28, 2026. The complete numerical cases here are original and supplied on this page.

heads: Write Jo's first-month payment instructions

Completed recommendation: “I would start with A $25 and B $95 each month, subject to the final-balance adjustment. This covers both minimums and directs $50 extra to B's 19% balance. The supplied schedule costs $96.35 interest, $12.30 less than smallest-balance-first, while both finish in 11 months. I would review the budget if income changes rather than treating $120 as guaranteed forever.”

“Put all $120 on B” leaves A unpaid and does not follow the model. “Borrow to invest and use the profit” replaces a known repayment budget with an uncertain future outcome. Neither is the same plan with a faster payoff.

title: Decide whether borrowing solves the problem

heads: Decide whether credit meets a need on workable terms
Name the function and timing
Count future commitments as well as today’s access
prose: Borrowing meets a payment now by committing money later. A useful decision begins with the need and deadline, then compares confirmed alternatives and the whole obligation.

A need is the function that must be met in the situation. Owning an item immediately may be one way to meet it; confirmed temporary access can be another. An alternative is usable only if its suitability, dates and costs are established.

For a simple example, a free, suitable loaner confirmed until a purchase deadline may allow time to save. A hoped-for loaner with no availability date cannot be treated the same way. Later income cannot pay an earlier bill unless a workable arrangement actually supplies access in time.

Add every payment and separate fee once. Compare that total with the cash price to identify extra financing cost. Check the payment dates against available money and the repayment length against the period of intended use.

Approval is a lender’s decision about an application; it is different from a borrower’s assessment of whether repayments fit. A co-borrower shares obligations under the agreement. That person’s consent and resources cannot be assumed.

Use need → deadline → confirmed alternatives → total and payment timing → recommendation with a condition. Explain a delay’s consequences as well as borrowing’s consequences. Inventing a new job, gift or refund would change the evidence.

When you read the case: Read the access arrangement, saving dates and quotation together. The first check asks which confirmed fact makes an alternative possible. Later you will compare the financing cost and whether the payment sequence serves the course need.

heads: Start with the need and the deadline
prose: Credit can provide something before enough cash has been saved. It also commits future money. A useful decision begins with what is needed, when it is needed and what alternatives actually exist. You will compare a loan with a confirmed temporary solution and a saving plan.

Your final product is a short recommendation about getting required work boots before a supplied deadline. You will calculate the borrowing cost and test the timing of a cash alternative. You will not apply for credit or use personal information.

heads: Nico's device decision
prose: Nico is a fictional adult beginning a ten-month online certificate course. The course needs a device that meets its supplied technical requirements. This case does not claim those requirements belong to a real provider.

Device quotation: a suitable device costs $420, including all charges. A financing offer requires 18 monthly payments of $32, with the first due one month after purchase, plus a $20 setup fee paid today. No other fee applies if paid on time. The purchased device meets the requirements; its useful life is not guaranteed by the repayment term.

Nico's budget note: $100 is available today. After essential costs, $80 can be set aside at the end of each of the next four months. This amount is confirmed for the case. No later income is promised. Nico has no other device.

Equipment-library confirmation: “A suitable device is reserved for Nico from the course start until immediately after the fourth monthly saving deposit. There is no borrowing fee or deposit. It must be returned on that date. The same $420 purchase quotation is valid through that date.”
The equipment loaner and the money loan are different arrangements. The library lends an object to be returned; the financing offer lends purchasing power to be repaid in money.

heads: Test purpose, timing and cost
Separate a confirmed alternative from a hopeful one
Compare consequences across time
prose: First name the need, the job the purchase must do. Nico needs reliable access to a suitable device for the course. Owning it on day one is one possible way to meet that need, not the definition of the need itself. Separating access from ownership makes alternatives visible without dismissing the importance of the course.

Next mark the deadline. Money expected after a deadline cannot pay a bill due before it. Nico's fourth deposit arrives just before the loaner must be returned, and the quotation remains valid. Those details make the proposed sequence possible. If either were unknown, the plan would need verification rather than a confident promise.

Then calculate the whole obligation. Add every payment and separate fee, subtract the cash price to find the extra financing cost, and compare the duration with the intended use. Eighteen payments continue beyond a ten-month course. A useful purchase can still have costly or inconvenient terms; a label such as “education” does not settle affordability.

“Use a loaner” is helpful only when its suitability, dates and cost are known. “Work more hours” is not confirmed income unless the case supplies approved hours and take-home money. A sound recommendation names what is available and what remains uncertain. It does not solve every gap by assuming a gift, refund or new job.

A loan application may request identity, income, existing debts and credit information. Approval is a lender's decision; the lesson's ability to calculate a payment is not approval. A co-borrower shares contractual obligations, rather than merely acting as a reference. Never add another person to a plan as if their consent and repayment ability were supplied.

A payment that looks small can limit later choices. Conversely, delaying a genuinely necessary purchase without a workable alternative can interrupt learning or work. Compare the actual consequences of each feasible option. Use an explicit decision line: need → deadline → available alternatives → total and timing → recommendation.

Optional FCAC reading record: Buy now, pay later plans identifies instalment arrangements as credit with terms to inspect, including fees and payment timing. Read September 28, 2026. The supplied quotation controls this exercise; no real product application or outside reading is required.

heads: Meet the device need without inventing money
prose: Financing costs 18 × $32 + $20 = $596. Compared with the $420 cash price, the extra cost is $176. Nico could pay the setup fee from the $100, but a first payment that fits today says little about all 18 future payments when only four months of available money are confirmed.

With the loaner, Nico retains the $100 and saves 4 × $80 = $320. The total reaches $420 at the fourth deposit. The loaner covers the time until then. This plan uses the specific confirmation, not a general assumption that equipment libraries always have stock.

Complete recommendation: “I recommend using the reserved loaner while setting aside $80 at each of the next four month-ends. With $100 already available, Nico reaches $420 before returning it and can use the valid cash quotation. Financing would total $596, $176 more, and continue for eight months beyond the course. I would confirm any changed loaner date or price before relying on this sequence.”

“Wait four months without a device” ignores the immediate learning need. “The $32 payment is cheap, so borrow” ignores total cost and the unconfirmed later budget. The model explains how access, not just money, is maintained.

title: Give a savings goal a job

heads: Give savings an amount, a purpose and a deadline
Find the gap and count the contributions
Check the shared limit and changing allocations
prose: A savings goal turns “save more” into a plan you can check. Learn to calculate the remaining gap and compare all goals drawing on the same saving money.

A target is the required total. An opening amount is money already assigned to that goal. The gap is target minus that assigned amount. The time horizon is how long remains before the money is needed.

In a simple example, a $90 target with $30 already saved leaves $60. Three remaining saving dates require $20 on each for an even plan. Count contributions actually available before the deadline, not every date on the calendar.

A shared limit is the total available for all the goals together. If one needs $20 weekly and another $10, the combined requirement is $30. A $25 weekly budget cannot fund both even plans as written, although either calculation works by itself.

An allocation assigns part of the available money to a purpose. When one goal is funded, its contribution can move to another goal if the timeline permits. Carry forward money already saved rather than counting it twice.

Use purpose and date → gap → contributions → combined limit → checkpoint balances. Keep a separately protected emergency reserve separate. Short-term targets should not rely on an assumed investment gain arriving by the deadline.

When you read the case: Read the goal board for the target, amount already assigned and saving dates. The first check asks for one remaining gap. Later, test whether the goals work together and redirect contributions after a goal is complete.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: A goal needs an amount, a date and a contribution
prose: “Save more” is an intention. A workable savings goal says what the money is for, how much is still needed, when it will be used and where each contribution will come from. You will build a plan for two goals sharing the same weekly money.
Your final product is an eight-week saving instruction for a fictional learner with a fee deadline and a competing hobby goal. No real account, personal budget or outside research is required.

How to complete this lesson: Read Sam's savings board and the money note. Learn Find the gap, then schedule it, follow a plan that changes after the first goal is finished, and test a lower weekly amount. Answer six questions. Complete Lena's fee deadline, compare with the model, revise and sign off. Pause after the first plan if needed; your work saves.

heads: Sam's savings board
prose: Sam is fictional. The board separates money by purpose so the same dollars are not promised twice. The figures below are all-in prices for this exercise and remain unchanged during the plan. No interest is included.

Weekly money note: Sam has $35 at the end of each week to share between these goals, after other costs. A separate $120 emergency reserve is for unexpected essential costs and is not available for the jacket or bicycle in this plan. The week-6 and week-12 deposits arrive before the respective purchase deadlines. The bicycle deadline can be moved if the plan cannot meet it; the jacket deadline cannot.

A savings board is a record of targets and contributions, not a bank statement or a claim that all the money already exists. “Already set aside” is the opening balance for that goal. Future weekly deposits still have to happen.
tables: Goal Money needed Already set aside for this goal Deadline Suitable winter jacket $180 $60 End of week 6 Used bicycle, with necessary equipment included $360 $120 End of week 12

heads: Find the gap, then schedule it
Change contributions when a goal is finished
Give emergency money a distinct purpose
prose: A savings goal combines a purpose, target amount and date. The gap is target minus money already allocated. Divide that gap by the available saving periods to find an even contribution. For Sam's jacket, $120 divided by six weekly deposits is $20 per week.

The bicycle gap is $360 − $120 = $240. Dividing by twelve gives $20 weekly. Each calculation works alone, but together they require $40 a week. Sam has only $35. This is the central planning check: add all contributions sharing one budget before declaring either plan feasible.

A plan need not use the same contribution forever. Once the jacket reaches its target after week six, its $20 weekly allocation becomes available for another purpose. You can redirect money already in the budget without inventing extra income. A timeline helps reveal when that becomes possible.

Use three lines in a plan: opening balance + scheduled contributions = balance at the checkpoint. Check both each goal and each week's total. A final balance that looks right is insufficient if the plan overspends along the way.

Saving often supports near-term purchases or unexpected costs where access and stability matter. Investing can support longer-term goals, but values may change and money may not be readily available on a particular date. Do not solve a six-week shortfall by assuming an investment will rise by the exact missing amount.

A separate emergency reserve is not “unused” money merely because it has no purchase date. It has a different job. If a real emergency requires using it, the plan should record that decision and later review replenishment. This case deliberately keeps it separate so the two purchase goals can be evaluated honestly.

Optional reference note: FCAC's Setting savings and investment goals connects a goal's time horizon with appropriate planning. Read September 28, 2026. The on-page board and weekly note supply all required facts; you do not need to browse products.

heads: Keep both goals within $35 a week
prose: For weeks 1–6, put $20 into the jacket goal and $15 into the bicycle goal. Each week totals $35. The jacket reaches $60 + 6 × $20 = $180 on time. The bicycle reaches $120 + 6 × $15 = $210.

After the jacket is funded, direct up to $35 weekly to the bicycle. Weeks 7–10 add $140, bringing it to $350. Only $10 more is needed in week 11, so the bicycle reaches $360 then. The remaining $25 from that week's $35 can stay unallocated for a later decision; it is not silently spent or counted in both goals.

Completed plan: “Save $20 for the jacket and $15 for the bicycle in each of weeks 1–6. The jacket is fully funded at week 6. Then save $35 for the bicycle in weeks 7–10 and the last $10 in week 11. Both deadlines are met without using the $120 emergency reserve or exceeding $35 in any week.”
The first pair of separate $20 plans was not wrong arithmetic; it was incomplete coordination. The revised plan keeps the deadlines and shows how contributions move after a goal is met.

title: Choose what the next dollar does

heads: Understand the different jobs money can do
Compare purpose, access and uncertainty
Name the alternative you give up
prose: The next available dollar can support a purchase, a reserve, debt repayment or investment. Learn what each use changes before comparing the supplied choices.

Spending buys a good, service or experience. Saving sets money aside for a purpose. Debt repayment reduces an obligation. Investing places money in assets with possible gains and losses. The label alone does not establish suitability.

Liquidity concerns how readily value becomes available money, including time and cost. A reserve may need ready access. An extra debt payment may save future interest while leaving less accessible cash; whether it can be borrowed back depends on the actual terms.
Identify money available for this new choice after the commitments already protected. Do not reallocate rent or a reserve the case says must remain separate.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best feasible alternative given up when choosing. It is not the sum of every rejected option. If $20 can either build a reserve or reduce debt, choosing the reserve postpones that debt reduction. The same $20 cannot do both at once.

A return is a gain or loss relative to money invested, considering relevant costs. A pair of possible investment outcomes illustrates uncertainty; it does not establish their probabilities or promise the favourable one.
Use available money → purpose and deadline → access and risk → feasible alternatives → chosen use and opportunity cost. Explain the trade-off using the priorities actually supplied.

When you read the case: Read the budget note to locate the amount being newly allocated, then the access and outcome records. The first check identifies which money is available. Later you will choose its purpose and explain the next-best alternative postponed.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: One amount cannot do every job at once
prose: Spending, saving, repaying debt and investing can each serve a purpose. The useful question is which purpose takes priority with the money actually available. You will explain a choice and its opportunity cost: the next-best alternative given up.

Your final product is a decision note for a fictional learner choosing between a necessary repair, an outing and a speculative investment idea. You will identify the amount needed, the priority and what is forgone. You do not need personal financial information.

How to complete this lesson: Read Avery's $80 decision, learn Compare purposes before returns, and follow a recommendation using Avery's stated priorities. Practise with one changed condition. Answer six checks, then complete Jules's repair decision. Compare, revise and sign off. Your entries save, and you can pause after the guided comparison.

heads: Avery's $80 decision
prose: Avery is a fictional adult with $80 unallocated today, after essentials and required debt payments. This is the only extra money available for this decision.

Situation note: Avery has $20 in an accessible emergency reserve and wants that reserve to reach $100. A separate debt balance is $300 at a fixed 18% annual rate. Its required payment is already covered in the budget. Extra principal payments are allowed without a fee. Reducing its balance reduces later interest under unchanged terms.
Available choices:

Avery's priorities, supplied for this case: First bring the emergency reserve to $100; then reduce costly debt; then consider long-term investing. The investment is not needed to meet a particular deadline.

heads: Compare purposes before returns
Name the next-best alternative
Test claims about return
prose: Saving sets money aside for a purpose, often with access and stability important for near-term needs. Investing puts money into assets with possible income or growth, alongside risks and possible losses. Debt repayment reduces an obligation. Spending buys a good, service or experience. None of these words alone proves a choice is suitable.

Ask when the money may be needed and what happens if it is unavailable or worth less. Avery's reserve needs ready access. The investment scenarios do not guarantee $80 will be available when an emergency occurs. Even a possible higher return does not answer the access question.

An extra debt payment can avoid future interest under the loan's terms, but it also moves cash into a use that may not be reversible. This case expressly says Avery cannot borrow that paid amount back. A decision about debt and saving therefore compares both cost and access.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when you choose. It is not automatically the sticker price and not the sum of every rejected option. Use the person's stated priorities to identify the next-best feasible option.

For Avery, if the reserve receives $80, the next-best use is extra debt repayment. The opportunity cost includes the debt reduction and associated interest saving delayed by choosing the reserve. The uncertain investment is a further alternative, not an additional opportunity cost to add to the debt repayment as though both could have been chosen with the same $80.

You can recognise a tradeoff without declaring a choice wrong. “This builds access, but postpones debt reduction” is a more useful explanation than “saving is always good.” Different priorities or circumstances can justify a different allocation.

A return is the gain or loss from an investment relative to money invested, considering relevant costs. Avery's $100 scenario would be a $20 gain before any costs outside the stated model; the $60 scenario would be a $20 loss. They demonstrate uncertainty, not the probability of either outcome. A sales headline showing only the gain is incomplete evidence.

Optional reading record: FCAC's Basics of investing identifies goals, time, financial circumstances, risk and costs as relevant to an investment decision. Read September 28, 2026. The case supplies all required choices and priorities; no live product research is required here.

heads: Apply Avery's stated priority
prose: The reserve gap is $100 − $20 = $80, exactly the unallocated amount. Putting all $80 there reaches the first priority without touching required payments. Debt stays at $300 for now; the extra repayment is postponed, not somehow achieved as well.

Complete decision note: “I would put the $80 in Avery's accessible reserve, bringing it from $20 to $100. This meets the first stated priority and keeps money available for an unexpected cost. The next-best alternative forgone is an extra $80 debt payment, which would have reduced the balance to $220 and reduced later interest. I would review extra debt repayment with the next genuinely available amount rather than assume the investment will fund both goals.”

“Choose the investment because it becomes $100” leaves out the $60 scenario and other possible values. “Save $80 and repay $80” spends $160 when only $80 is available. The model's strength is that it states what remains unfinished.

title: Separate an account from what it holds

heads: Separate the account from the investment inside it
Read the two layers
Compare the holding with the goal
prose: An account arrangement and a holding describe different parts of an investment decision. Learn both layers before reading the options.

An account arrangement supplies rules around eligible holdings. A holding is where the money is placed. A TFSA is an account arrangement with tax rules; a GIC is a holding with stated repayment and interest conditions. “A GIC held in a TFSA” names both layers.

An account name does not supply a holding’s rate, guarantee its value or make locked money accessible. The supplied case states the account eligibility and room needed here; no personal tax information is required.

Liquidity describes how readily value becomes available money. Risk includes possible loss or failure to meet the goal. Return includes gains, losses and income, after relevant costs. A fee reduces what is kept. Read how and when money can be withdrawn or sold.

A holding saleable on a deadline may still have an uncertain sale value. A holding with a stated repayment date may not be accessible earlier. First identify when money is needed and what happens if it is worth less or unavailable.
Use goal and date → holding’s access, risk, return and fees → account rules → choice and remaining uncertainty. A willingness to take risk is different from having enough resources to bear a loss.

When you read the case: Identify which record names an account arrangement and which names a holding before the first check. Later you will use the goal’s deadline and the supplied access terms to evaluate a combination of the two.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Two different choices are hiding in one question
prose: “Should I use a Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) or buy a Guaranteed Investment Certificate (GIC)?” mixes an account arrangement with a product. A suitable account may hold different investments, each with different access, fees and risks. You will separate those choices and use product records to match money to a purpose.

Your final product is a two-goal comparison for a fictional adult. Choose an appropriate place for near-term money, explain a possible long-term holding, and check a supplied account limit. You will not open an account or disclose a real tax record.

How to complete this lesson: Read Noor's two decisions and Account and product reference. Learn how the two layers work, follow the near-term example and practise a changed goal. Answer six questions. Complete Milan's two goals, compare, revise and sign off. All required product information is supplied; official links are optional.

heads: Noor's two decisions
Account and product reference
prose: Noor is a fictional 19-year-old with $500 needed for a confirmed course fee in six months. Losing part of that money or being unable to withdraw it at the deadline would prevent payment. Noor is comparing the following invented product records, all available in a non-registered account or the provider's TFSA for this exercise.

The product labels are shortcuts: S means savings deposit, G means the one-year GIC and F means equity fund. They name the three holdings in the table, not account types or grades. Read the access and risk column before comparing returns.

Account note: Noor's eligibility to open the case TFSA and $1,000 remaining contribution room are explicitly confirmed for the exercise. That is Noor's fictional remaining room, not a current annual limit for everyone. No contributions or withdrawals occur except those described. A non-registered account has no TFSA contribution-room restriction but does not receive TFSA tax treatment.

The following short record summarizes selected Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) plan distinctions, read September 28, 2026. It is enough for this lesson; actual eligibility, room and withdrawal conditions must be checked before a real transaction.
