heads: Tess's move-in folder
prose: Tess is a fictional adult planning a first move. Tess has $1,250 available by September 1. All listed starting amounts are due by that date. No loan, overdraft or additional money is available unless a later practice update explicitly supplies it.
Room offer — September 1 start

Room contribution: $480 for September, then $480 monthly. Deposit: $480, held separately and refundable at the end if the stated return conditions are met. It cannot be used to pay the next month's room contribution. Utilities are additional; the provider's quote has not arrived. This invented agreement is a cost-reading example, not a statement of Alberta tenancy law.
Starting checklist with quotes

Tess expects $900 net income each month after moving. This is a supplied planning assumption, not a guarantee about employment. Other living expenses are outside this simplified exercise and would need investigation in a real plan.

heads: Sort costs by what happens to the money
Give an unknown its own line
Change the plan deliberately
prose: An upfront cost is due at the beginning. A recurring cost repeats, such as a monthly transit pass. A refundable deposit ties up money now with a possible later return under specified conditions. These categories can overlap: the first monthly payment is both an upfront cash requirement and part of an ongoing cost. Count it once in the period being analysed.

An ownership or use cost is something needed to keep using the purchase or arrangement: maintenance, storage, utilities, insurance or interest, depending on the situation. A vehicle's advertised price, for example, does not include every future insurance, maintenance and operating expense. The relevant amounts require quotes and a time period; guessing that they are zero hides rather than resolves the uncertainty.

Use two views. Cash needed by the start date includes every payment due then, including a deposit. Cost over the use period separates money expected back from money used up, and states return assumptions. A deposit can affect affordability even when it is not a permanent expense.

An unknown is a missing figure, not a zero. A known minimum is the total of amounts already established. If the known minimum exceeds available money, you can identify a problem without knowing every extra cost. If it fits, you still cannot call the plan fully affordable until material unknowns are resolved or a justified allowance is supplied.

A quote should state what it includes, how long it applies and when payment is due. “Utilities around something small” is not a quote. “$65 for this month's supplied utility package, due September 1” is usable in a dated exercise.

A shortfall can be addressed by reducing an optional cost, choosing a different arrangement, delaying the start or adding confirmed resources. Each change has consequences. A cheaper setup might be suitable; skipping necessary food is not an equivalent saving. Promised extra hours that have not been scheduled cannot be counted as confirmed money.

Cost map: start-date payments → accessible money remaining → repeated monthly commitments → irregular/unknown costs → decision and condition. This keeps “Can I start?” separate from “Can I keep doing it?”

Optional Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) note, read September 28, 2026: distinguish an unexpected expense from an occasional expense that can be planned. A known monthly storage bill belongs in the plan before an emergency occurs. “Setting up an emergency fund”.

heads: Find Tess's known move-in requirement
prose: By September 1, Tess must have $480 room + $480 deposit + $75 transit + $160 setup + $190 food = $1,385, before utilities. Available money is $1,250, so the known amounts already exceed it by $135. The refundable deposit is still needed on the start date.

I also look beyond move-in. Known repeated costs are $480 + $75 + $190 = $745 monthly, plus utilities and any other relevant costs outside this exercise. The $480 deposit and $160 setup are not repeated each month. Comparing $900 income with $745 gives $155 before those remaining costs, not $155 guaranteed spare spending.

Completed note: “Tess needs at least $1,385 by September 1, $135 more than the $1,250 available, and utilities are still unknown. The move cannot be treated as funded on the supplied figures. I would obtain the utility quote and examine a lower setup cost or different start arrangement before committing. Known recurring costs are $745 per month; the $155 difference from assumed income must still cover utilities and other relevant costs.”
“The room is only $480, so Tess has $770 spare” ignores the rest of the move-in folder. “Utilities cost zero because no number is written” turns missing information into an invented fact.

title: Test a fixed or variable rate

heads: Separate the interest-rate rule from the payment rule
Know what is fixed and what can change
Test the payment and the total separately
prose: A fixed or variable rate describes how interest can change. It does not, by itself, explain what happens to the monthly payment. Read both rules before interpreting a loan comparison.

A fixed rate stays the same for the specified period. A variable rate can change under the agreement. A rate reset is the point where the model applies a new rate. Some agreements recalculate the payment; others can hold the payment while changing its split or repayment length.

The case’s written payment rule determines which behaviour to use. A recalculated payment uses the remaining balance and remaining repayment months, because earlier payments have already reduced the debt.

A payment margin is available repayment money minus the required payment. With an invented $45 limit and $40 payment, the margin is $5. If a scenario raises the payment to $50, there is a $5 gap. A lower initial payment does not establish that later ones fit.

A stress test here means checking a less favourable supplied scenario. It is not a prediction of what rates will do or a lender’s approval procedure. Hold principal, payment frequency, repayment length and fees steady when comparing the rate paths.
Use rate rule → payment-change rule → supplied scenario outputs → margin in each period → total cost → recommendation. Keep a scenario’s possible outcome separate from a forecast or guarantee.

When you read the case: Read what the variable agreement says happens when its rate changes. The first check asks about that payment behaviour. Later, compare the complete supplied rate paths and the budget margins rather than choosing from month one alone.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: A starting rate is only the beginning
prose: Two loans can start with different payments and finish with different costs. You will compare a fixed-rate agreement with a variable-rate agreement under two supplied rate paths. A scenario lets you test a possibility; it does not predict future rates.

Your final product is a recommendation using a new pair of fictional loans, their calculated outputs and a monthly limit. Explain both cost and uncertainty. No outside rate search or loan application is required.

How to complete this lesson: Read Ari's two quotations and their calculation rules. Learn Read what changes when the rate changes, follow the first comparison, then test a higher second-year rate. Answer six checks. Complete Jules's three-year comparison, compare your reasoning and sign off. Pause after the stress scenario if helpful; your work saves.

heads: Ari's two quotations
prose: Ari, a fictional adult, needs to compare financing for the same $5,000 purchase over 24 months. Both agreements have no setup fee, insurance charge or other fee under on-time repayment. Interest uses nominal annual rate/12 each month; payments occur at month-end. No additional advances occur. Ari has $223 a month available for this loan, after other planned costs.

Names used in this comparison: F means Ari's fixed-rate offer; V means Ari's variable-rate offer. The 5%-then-7% scenario shows one possible rate change for the variable offer. These letters only help you find the matching quotation; they are not ratings.
Fixed offer F: 6% annually for all 24 months. Regular payment $221.60; final payment $221.69; total payments $5,318.49; interest $318.49.

Variable offer V: begins at 5%. If its rate changes at month 13, the payment is recalculated to repay the remaining balance over the remaining 12 months. This agreement changes the payment, not the original finish date. Its first 12 payments are $219.36.

Supplied 5%-then-7% scenario: 5% for months 1–12, then 7% for months 13–24. The recalculated regular payment is $221.71; the final payment is $221.70. Total payments are $5,292.83 and interest is $292.83. This is one possible path, not a quotation promising next year's rate.

heads: Read what changes when the rate changes
Hold the comparison steady
Test a budget and a cost separately
prose: A fixed rate remains the same for the specified contract period. A variable rate can change according to its agreement. These terms describe the interest rate; you must also read what happens to the payment or repayment period. In Ari's variable agreement, a change triggers a new payment calculated over the months still remaining.

Other agreements may hold a payment temporarily constant, which changes how much goes to principal as interest changes. Do not assume that “variable” always means the same payment behaviour. The written rule in the case is essential information, not fine print to skip.

A lower starting rate can be attractive, but comparing only month one leaves out future payments. Compare the entire supplied scenario and test a less favourable one. A higher future rate may reduce the original saving or reverse it. A fixed rate offers rate certainty during its stated period; it does not eliminate income changes, missed-payment consequences or every other risk.

Use the same principal, repayment length, payment frequency and fee assumptions when isolating a rate choice. Otherwise, a lower payment might be caused by a longer period or smaller loan rather than the rate. Our comparison holds those features constant.

The calculator first pays down the balance at the starting rate. At month 13 it uses the remaining balance, not the original $5,000, for the recalculation. This matters because twelve payments have already reduced principal. We supply complete output records so you can analyse the decision without deriving the payment formula.

Subtract the required payment from the available monthly amount to find the payment margin. A positive margin means the stated payment fits that stated limit. A small margin provides little room if another cost changes. It does not prove the whole financial situation is secure.

Then compare total payments and interest. A loan may have a smaller total under one rate path but a later payment that fails the budget under another. Keep those findings separate so your recommendation can explain the tradeoff clearly.

Optional source note: FCAC distinguishes fixed rates, variable rates and different payment arrangements. Its Choosing a mortgage rate section is an example of why rate type and payment behaviour must both be read. Ari's case is a fictional instalment agreement, not a mortgage or a forecast of lender practice. No outside page is needed.

heads: Compare the fixed offer with the 5%-then-7% scenario
prose: F's regular payment leaves $223 − $221.60 = $1.40 monthly margin. Its $221.69 final payment also fits. The 5%-then-7% scenario begins with $3.64 margin and later leaves $223 − $221.71 = $1.29. Both fit the supplied budget in this scenario, but neither leaves much room.
Interest in the 5%-then-7% scenario is $292.83 compared with F's $318.49. The difference is $25.66. That comparison includes the whole supplied path and the final adjusted payments.

Completed comparison: “With a 5%-then-7% path, V costs $25.66 less interest than F, and its payments fit Ari's $223 limit. However, the 7% later rate is a scenario, not guaranteed. F fixes its rate for the full 24 months and also fits, with a small margin. I would test a higher later rate before deciding whether the possible saving is worth the uncertainty.”

“V will definitely save $25.66” removes the condition that made the calculation true. “Fixed means cheaper” is also unsupported: the supplied 5%-then-7% scenario costs less. The correct explanation preserves both the observed numbers and their limits.
Next: Test a 10% second year. Try “Regular payment amount above Ari's limit ($)” before opening its comparison model.

title: Read a mortgage beyond its monthly payment

heads: A mortgage term and amortization are different clocks
Read the contract and repayment plan separately
Look beyond the quoted payment
prose: A mortgage quotation can describe one contract period and a much longer planned repayment period. Learn that distinction before reading the quotation’s payment and balance figures.

The term is the period for which the current mortgage agreement applies. The amortization is the planned time to repay through scheduled payments under the model’s assumptions. A two-year term within a ten-year amortization would not mean the full loan is paid off after two years or the same rate is promised for ten.

The remaining balance is debt still owing at a stated date. At the end of a term, it must be addressed through repayment or an appropriate further agreement. A long-run calculator illustration keeping one rate is a conditional model.

A principal-and-interest payment covers those loan components. Housing can also involve taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance and transaction costs. Check what a supplied budget limit already includes before using it.

A prepayment is principal paid beyond scheduled payments. A prepayment privilege states permitted amounts and timing without a specified charge. If it uses a percentage, identify the base: original principal, remaining balance and property value are different amounts.

Use borrowed money → contract-period payments → remaining debt at term end → costs outside the payment → flexibility conditions. A payment calculation alone does not establish loan approval or complete housing affordability.

When you read the case: Locate the term and amortization separately in the quotation. The first check asks what ends at the stated term date. Later you will explain remaining debt and compare the supplied prepayment conditions without assuming an unchanged renewal rate.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Five years can be part of a twenty-five-year plan
prose: A mortgage quotation can name both a five-year term and a twenty-five-year amortization. Those numbers answer different questions. You will read them alongside the down payment, remaining balance and rules for extra payments.

Your final product is a comparison note for two fictional mortgage quotations. Explain the payment, balance at the end of the term and a planned extra payment. This is a document-reading exercise, not a recommendation to buy a home or a mortgage approval.

How to complete this lesson: Read Lee and Noor's quotation, learn Separate the contract from the repayment plan, and follow the five-year calculation. Practise changing amortization. Answer six checks. Compare Morgan's two quotations, revise your note and sign off. The full text and schedules are provided; live lender contact is not required. Pause after the first comparison if useful.

heads: Lee and Noor's quotation
prose: Lee and Noor are fictional adults considering a teaching-example property price of $160,000. They have $40,000 for a down payment, leaving $120,000 mortgage principal. Other purchase and ownership costs have a separate allocation and are excluded from this loan-only illustration; their exclusion does not mean homes have no taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs or legal costs.

Quotation M: fixed 6% nominal annual interest compounded semi-annually, monthly payments, five-year term and 25-year amortization. Regular payment: $767.77. During the first 60 months, scheduled payments total $46,066.20, of which $33,870.12 is interest. The balance after payment 60 is $107,803.92. No extra payment or fee is included in these outputs.

Extra-payment condition: up to 10% of original principal per contract year may be paid in one additional lump sum without a prepayment charge. Unused allowance does not carry forward. A larger extra payment may incur a charge whose calculation must be requested. These are invented terms for this quotation, not a rule for every mortgage.

A mortgage is borrowing secured on property. Failing to meet its terms can put that property at risk. Down payment means the buyer's contribution to the purchase price; it is not the same as a regular loan payment.

heads: Separate the contract from the repayment plan
Know what the payment leaves out
Read flexibility as carefully as the rate
prose: The term is how long the current mortgage agreement applies. Its rate and other conditions are established for that period. At the end, any unpaid balance must be addressed: for example, by repayment or an appropriate new agreement. Do not assume renewal has the same rate.

The amortization is the planned time over which scheduled payments would repay the loan under the model's assumptions. It can be much longer than one term. A five-year term within a 25-year amortization therefore does not promise the same rate for 25 years. A long-run calculator illustration holding a rate constant must say that it is conditional.

Read a quotation as three connected records: money borrowed today → payments during this contract → debt still owing when the contract ends. The remaining balance explains why someone may still need financing after years of payments.

A quoted principal-and-interest payment is not necessarily the entire cost of housing. Taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance and transaction costs may be separate. This exercise supplies a loan-payment limit only after those other costs have been considered; you cannot reuse it as a real affordability approval.

An application may require evidence of income, down payment, existing debts and credit history. The lender assesses its current criteria and the property. Knowing the payment is only part of that assessment. Do not upload personal records or infer eligibility from this fictional calculation.

A prepayment is money paid toward principal beyond scheduled payments. A prepayment privilege is the amount and timing the contract permits without a specified charge. Some agreements are more flexible than others. A percentage needs a base: M uses original principal, so its 10% allowance is based on $120,000, not the current balance or property price.

Extra principal paid earlier can reduce later interest under unchanged terms, but the amount, timing and any charge matter. This lesson compares permission only; its schedules contain no extra payments. Do not use an unchanged schedule to claim the precise saving from a proposed prepayment.

Optional official reading record: FCAC's mortgage guidance distinguishes contract term, amortization and prepayment conditions. Read September 28, 2026. It supports these reading questions; the complete fictional quotation supplies the numbers and conditions used here.

heads: Explain the balance after five years
prose: The initial loan is $160,000 − $40,000 = $120,000. Sixty regular payments total 60 × $767.77 = $46,066.20. However, not all of that pays down principal: $33,870.12 is interest. Principal repaid is $46,066.20 − $33,870.12 = $12,196.08. Subtracting that from $120,000 leaves $107,803.92, matching the schedule.
M's annual extra-payment allowance is 10% × $120,000 = $12,000. It does not mean $12,000 is available in Lee and Noor's budget; it is a contract permission.

Complete explanation: “M fixes its rate for five years, while payments are calculated over a 25-year repayment plan. After the first five years, $107,803.92 remains because only $12,196.08 of the $46,066.20 paid reduced principal. The contract allows a lump sum up to $12,000 in each contract year without the stated prepayment charge. Future rates and any actual extra-payment saving require a new calculation.”
“The balance must be $73,933.80 because they paid $46,066.20” incorrectly treats interest as principal repayment. The schedule makes the split visible.
Next: Shorten amortization to 20 years. Try “Increase in regular monthly payment ($)” before opening its comparison model.

title: Revise a plan when life changes

heads: Revise from the money and time remaining now
Start from the current balance
Change a condition openly
prose: A plan needs revision when actual events change its assumptions. Learn to separate what has already happened from what remains possible before reading the changed savings record.

A transaction is a movement such as a deposit or payment. The current balance reflects transactions already made. A plan variance is a difference between the plan and what actually happened. A revised projection starts from the new facts rather than rewriting earlier ones.

For a simple example, after an expense the current balance is $90, the target is $150 and two deposits remain. The gap is $60, so an even plan requires $30 per remaining deposit. An old opening balance or elapsed contribution date cannot be reused as though the expense and time had not occurred.

A revision can change the contribution, target, deadline or a confirmed resource. A higher contribution must fit the budget; a reduced target must still meet the need; a later deadline must actually be flexible. A hoped-for gift or price recovery is not a confirmed resource.
Keep a one-time cost separate from ongoing costs. Name which condition changes and why, then state a review trigger: an event that would require another check.

Use actual event → present balance → remaining gap and saving dates → feasible change → review. These required saving cases assume no interest. Any optional growth investigation is a separate model and does not supply extra money for them.

When you read the case: Read the actual contributions and expense before the revised budget. The first check asks for the balance immediately after the event. Later you will count only the remaining saving dates and explain an adjustment that fits the supplied limits.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

heads: Keep the record; change the next action
prose: A plan can be reasonable when written and still need revision after an unexpected cost. You will separate what has already happened from what can change next. The task is to recalculate from the actual balance, explain the adjustment and set a new review point.

Your final product is a revision note for a fictional saving plan after a necessary expense. It will show the current balance, remaining gap and feasible future contributions. No personal loss, income or account information is required.

How to complete this lesson: Read Ari's original plan and transaction record, learn Update from the present balance, and follow a revised contribution. Practise a flexible deadline and optionally test a monthly budget shock. Answer six checks. Complete Devon's changed plan, compare, revise and sign off. All entries save; the original record remains visible.

heads: Ari's original plan and transaction record
prose: Ari is fictional and wants $350 by the end of month 6 for a purchase. The plan began with $200, then scheduled $25 at each of six month-ends. No interest or fee applies. The deadline was initially treated as fixed.
What actually happened:

New budget information: Ari can normally save $30 in each remaining month after other costs. A confirmed temporary change can instead free up to $45 monthly for months 3–6, without missing essential costs or required payments. There is no other money available. The repair has already been paid and is not refundable in the case.
tables: Event Change Balance Start Opening $200 $200 End of month 1 Deposit $25 $225 End of month 2 Deposit $25 $250 Immediately after month 2 Necessary repair, withdrawal $80 $170

heads: Update from the present balance
Change a constraint openly
Review goals as circumstances change
prose: A revision changes a future action in response to evidence. It does not rewrite earlier transactions. Start with the actual balance, subtract it from the target and count the deposits still available before the deadline. This creates a new gap and a new required contribution.

For Ari, two months have passed. Only four month-end deposits remain before month six. Using six deposits in the revised calculation would pretend time already elapsed is still available. Similarly, restarting at the old $200 balance would erase both saving progress and the repair cost.

There are several possible levers: contribution, target amount, deadline or a confirmed resource. Each has consequences. A higher contribution must fit the revised budget. A lower target must still meet the need. A later date must actually be flexible. A resource must be confirmed rather than hoped for.

Sometimes no combination satisfies every original condition. Naming the conflict is better planning than hiding it. A revision note should say which condition changes and why. It should also distinguish a temporary adjustment from an ongoing one so that next month's plan does not accidentally repeat a one-time cost.

Education, work, relocation, family responsibilities and retirement can change a person's purposes, time horizons and ability to take risk. A plan made for one life stage may need different priorities later. Reviewing does not mean changing every goal whenever a headline appears; it means checking relevant evidence against the decision's assumptions.

For investments, a market value change can affect a plan without being a deposit or withdrawal. A $500 holding worth $450 has depreciated by $50; that record does not reveal whether it will recover. Keep contributions, withdrawals, fees and market changes distinct. A short-term bill should not rely on an assumed rebound.

A useful revision note follows actual event → present balance → remaining need and time → feasible change → review trigger. This is the second representation of the method; each part will appear in your final response.

Optional reference: FCAC's budget guidance recommends comparing a plan with actual income and spending and updating it as circumstances change. Read September 28, 2026. All required records and alternatives in this lesson are supplied.
Want to explore growth on earlier growth? The optional FINLIT compounding investigation uses a separate 40-year model. Ari’s and Devon’s saving plans here still assume no interest.

heads: Keep Ari's month-six deadline
prose: After the repair, the balance is $170. The target gap is $350 − $170 = $180. With four deposits remaining, $180 ÷ 4 = $45 monthly is required.

The normal $30 amount would add only $120, ending at $290 and leaving $60 short. The supplied temporary budget change permits $45, so the revised plan can still meet the deadline. This conclusion relies on that confirmation; it does not assume every person can simply save more.

Complete revision: “The $80 repair leaves $170 after month two. To reach $350 at month six, Ari needs another $180 across four deposits, or $45 monthly. I would use the confirmed temporary adjustment for months 3–6 and check after month 3 that the first revised deposit happened and the $45 remains available. If it no longer fits, I would revisit a flexible date or target rather than erase the repair from the record.”

“Continue $25 and everything is fine” ignores the changed balance. “Start the original six-month plan again” changes the deadline without saying so. A complete revision preserves both the history and the condition being changed.

title: Compare the promise, the price and the terms

heads: Compare the advertised promise with the written terms
Hold the purchase details steady
Write a concern that can be investigated
prose: A consumer concern becomes clearer when the advertisement, price and accepted terms are compared on the same basis. Learn to label those records before reading the supplied offer.

A mandatory fee must be paid to obtain the stated offer. An optional charge can be declined. Compare the same item, quantity and choices at each stage, and keep before-tax and after-tax prices separate.

For a simple invented offer, an advertisement says $40 before tax and checkout says $45 before tax for the unchanged item. The $5 difference is separate from tax. If it comes from a charge the customer cannot decline, name that required charge when explaining the concern.

A subscription term states the commitment and conditions. A monthly payment describes payment frequency; it does not alone establish that the agreement ends every month or can be cancelled without further obligations.

Use promise → conflicting record → effect → specific requested response. Identify dates, amounts and relevant wording. Preserve the available originals rather than replacing an earlier advertisement with a corrected one.

A merchant dispute concerns a recognized purchase or its terms. A transaction not made or approved by the person is a different fact pattern. Describe which occurred instead of treating every unwanted charge as unauthorized.

Choose a route for the job it can do: explaining or correcting the offer, addressing a payment concern, or reviewing a broader consumer issue. A request, acknowledgement and confirmed correction are separate statuses.

When you read the case: Read the advertisement and checkout for the same purchase and tax basis. The first check asks which fact supports the price concern. Later you will document the conflict, cancellation conditions where supplied and a suitable response route.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

A low advertised price can change when a shopper reaches checkout. A subscription can also sound flexible in an advertisement while a later term describes a costly commitment. A useful consumer response identifies the exact contradiction, preserves the documents and asks the right organization for the kind of help it can provide.

You will compare a tablet advertisement with a fully supplied checkout, write a supported response to a changed offer, and then prepare a new subscription-dispute file. Your final product will explain the disputed terms, include a clear message to the business, and choose suitable escalation routes without promising a refund.

Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Use the method with the case → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Pause after the price comparison if useful. All writing stays in the course; do not buy anything, contact a business or submit a complaint. The guided work and six questions are practice. The independent file and four sign-offs complete the lesson. Fields save automatically.

Vocabulary. An advertised price is the price presented to attract a purchaser. A mandatory fee is a charge the purchaser cannot decline while buying that offer. An optional addition can be declined. Drip pricing involves advertising an unattainable price because mandatory fixed fees are added later; the specific federal rule described here treats government-imposed charges on purchasers, such as sales tax, differently. A consumer dispute is a disagreement about a transaction or its terms. A remedy is a requested solution; requesting it does not establish that the business must provide it in every case.
Optional disclosure: Consumer-source records and live references. Everything needed is supplied below. Official live links are optional for checking a current real situation.

prose: Mina is a fictional adult in Alberta considering a tablet from Clearview Devices, a fictional business selling online from Alberta. Mina has reached checkout but has not agreed to purchase or paid. The tablet model and quantity are the same in each document. No accessory, delivery upgrade or other optional item was selected.
The tax amount is supplied so the receipt is complete. This lesson asks you to analyze the store fees, not infer or research a tax rate.

Competition Bureau, “Drip pricing”; checked September 28, 2026. The Bureau explains that an advertised price made unattainable by mandatory fixed fees is contrary to the Competition Act, apart from government-imposed charges on purchasers such as sales tax. Variable fees can also raise concerns. A report about deceptive marketing can be made through the Bureau's official site. An individual learner cannot determine a legal outcome from a short case.

Government of Alberta, “Unfair business practices”; checked September 28, 2026. Alberta's Consumer Protection Act addresses unfair practices, including misleading representations and pricing. Its protections can apply before, during or after a transaction, even when a purchase has not been completed. Keep the offer, terms, receipts and communications that show the concern. These fictional parties and the offer are in Alberta; this course does not generalize Alberta jurisdiction to every online purchase.

Government of Alberta, “File a consumer complaint against a business”; checked September 28, 2026. Start by trying to resolve a concern with the business and retain the record. Alberta's Consumer Investigations Unit assesses possible violations within its authority. The described complaint route begins with the Consumer Contact Centre and a complaint ID before the portal stage. The unit does not recover a consumer's financial losses, mediate the dispute or renegotiate the contract. A complaint is not a guaranteed refund procedure.

Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, “How credit cards work,” “Credit card purchases”; checked September 28, 2026. Compare the statement with receipts. For a mistake, contact the merchant; if the problem is not corrected, contact the financial institution for assistance. Explain the facts accurately. Disagreement with recognized purchase terms is different from saying a transaction was never made or approved.

heads: Compare the same offer at each stage
Read what a condition actually does
Build a concern that someone can investigate
Match the route to the job
prose: Begin with the product, quantity and choices. A difference caused by selecting a larger model or optional delivery does not establish the same issue as a required charge added to an unchanged offer. Mina's documents hold those details constant: one Cedar tablet, standard pickup and no optional additions.

Then compare prices on the same basis. The advertisement says $120 before tax; checkout says $150 before tax. Subtracting those amounts isolates the store-fee difference. Comparing $120 directly with the tax-inclusive $157.50 would mix the fee concern with a separate supplied tax line.

Write the arithmetic with labels. A dollar difference is useful evidence only when the reader understands what the two amounts represent. Do not replace the comparison with “the business is stealing”; that is an accusation about conduct or intent that these documents do not establish.

A condition matters when it changes a consumer's practical choice. A charge called “service,” “processing” or “setup” is still mandatory in this case because the customer cannot decline it. A small font or a final opportunity to abandon checkout does not make the advertised $120 purchase available.

Subscriptions require the same close reading. “Monthly payment” describes when money is charged; it does not by itself prove that the commitment lasts only one month. Compare statements about duration, renewal, cancellation and fees across the advertisement and the accepted terms. If they conflict, identify both statements. Do not hide an inconvenient term, and do not assume its presence automatically resolves a misleading-advertisement concern.

Use promise → conflicting document → effect → requested response. Name the date and document, quote only the short wording necessary, and state the amount or condition affected. Then ask for a specific response, such as an accurate written quote, correction of a disputed charge, or confirmation of cancellation terms. A focused request makes it easier to understand the disagreement.

Keep copies already available. A later corrected advertisement is useful new evidence but does not replace the earlier version in the chronology. A record should distinguish “requested a correction,” “business acknowledged the request” and “correction confirmed.” These are different stages.

The routes can serve different purposes for the same documents. There is no need to submit a report to every organization for every disagreement. Explain what assistance is being sought and whether a purchase or payment has even occurred.
Optional first-step hint: “Underline ‘before sales tax’ in both price records. Compare the two subtotals first, then name which fees account for the difference.”

prose: I check that Mina selected the same tablet and no extras. I then read the advertisement's promise: mandatory store fees are included in $120 before tax. The business reply confirms that both added fees are required and are not government charges. That removes two possible explanations—optional choices and tax—for the $30 difference.

My calculation is $25.00 + $5.00 = $30.00 in required store fees. Equivalently, $150.00 − $120.00 = $30.00 above the advertised pre-tax price. The supplied checkout total is consistent: $150.00 + $7.50 = $157.50. I do not subtract the full total from the advertised amount and call all of the difference a prohibited fee.
Complete concern and action note:

An unsupported alternative would say “the bank must refund $157.50.” Mina has paid nothing, and the sources do not establish an automatic refund. A useful response follows the actual stage of the transaction.

heads: Omar's subscription file
prose: Omar is a fictional 19-year-old Alberta resident. SoundShelf is a fictional Alberta online audio-library business. The issue concerns a recognized subscription and conflicting cancellation representations. No password theft, card theft or unfamiliar merchant is reported.
Document E — Advertisement saved October 1, 2026. “SoundShelf: $9 each month. Cancel anytime. No exit fee.” The same plan appears in the following records.

Document F — Checkout and accepted terms, October 1. The payment summary shows $9 due that day and future billing on the first day of each month. Below the summary, the terms say: “This plan has a twelve-month commitment. Ending before the commitment ends requires a $45 early-exit fee.” Omar accepted the checkout; the record does not say whether Omar noticed that sentence. The receipt shows the initial $9 payment and the same business name. No tax or other fee is part of this exercise.

Document G — Cancellation correspondence. On October 20, Omar wrote through the business contact on the saved receipt: “Please cancel before the November 1 renewal. Your advertisement said cancel anytime with no exit fee. Please confirm cancellation with no further charge.” On October 22, the business replied: “We will end the plan on November 1. We will charge the November $9 payment and a $45 early-exit fee under the commitment term. We will not waive either.” There is no further explanation of why another monthly payment is due after the October 20 request.

Document H — Statement and follow-up. The genuine card statement shows a November 1 SoundShelf charge of $54. On November 2, Omar sent the business the advertisement, October 20 request and statement and asked it to correct the $54 charge and confirm no future billing. On November 4, the business replied: “We stand by the October 22 reply. The subscription is closed; there will be no future monthly charges.” No refund is shown. The issuer is available through the existing physical card or genuine app. No issuer dispute has yet been opened. Every date is a supplied fictional case fact, even though the source records were checked earlier.

title: Coordinate a recovery plan

heads: Coordinate help around the actual exposure
Make an exposure map
Keep actions and outcomes distinct
prose: A recovery plan can involve several services, but each should have a reason to act. Learn to map the confirmed loss or information exposure to the provider that can address it.

A recovery plan connects risks with actions and follow-up. Identify categories actually involved: a payment, account credential, identity information or device access. Then identify the provider or official route with responsibility for that category.

For a simple example, a deceptive transfer and an exposed email password create a financial branch and an account-security branch. Reporting a payment does not change the password, and changing a password does not recover the payment. Additional agencies need a relevant reason, not merely the fact that an incident occurred.

A status log separates action planned, action taken with a time or reference, and confirmed result or next check. “Reported” does not mean “refunded.” “Password changed” does not mean “all other sessions ended.” Explain what is still unresolved.

Use confirmed exposure → time-sensitive protection → provider-specific requests → reporting where relevant → follow-up. Do not delay urgent contact to perfect a record. Use independently reached routes, not contact details supplied by the suspicious sender.

A recovery scam offers another deceptive rescue, often requesting a fee, code or secrecy. A promised recovery is not evidence of authority or success. Keep existing evidence safely and do not send another payment or code to prove entitlement to help.

When you read the case: Read the payment and credential events separately before matching routes. The first check asks which response fits a confirmed financial event. Later you will coordinate the account, reporting and follow-up actions and resist a second-loss request.
Next: Meet the first situation. The explanation above is for learning; your first answer comes after you have read the supplied records.

After fraud, a person may need several kinds of help. A bank can address a payment route; an email provider can address account access; police and fraud-reporting services have reporting roles. Sending one report does not automatically complete the other jobs. A calm plan assigns each action to the organization that can carry it out and records what has actually happened.

You will coordinate a response to a ticket-payment and password incident, update the plan when providers reply, and then build a distinct plan for identity information and an independently observed tax-account change. The final product is a prioritized response plan with specific recipients, safe routes, evidence and follow-up conditions.

Follow Meet the situation and read the documents → Use the method with the case → Follow a complete example → Practise with support → Check your understanding → Apply independently → Review and complete. Work in small parts and pause after the response table if useful. Everything happens in the fictional record. Do not open a real financial account, disclose a Social Insurance Number (SIN), contact an agency or ask another person to supervise. Guided work and six questions are practice; the new independent plan and sign-offs complete this lesson. Your writing saves automatically.

Vocabulary. Recovery is the process of responding to an incident and restoring security or addressing losses; it does not promise that money will be returned. An affected provider controls a relevant account or service. Identity fraud involves misuse of identity information; exposure and confirmed misuse should be distinguished. A credit report records credit information; a fraud alert asks potential creditors to take additional identity-verification steps. A recovery scam offers to recover losses as a way to demand more money, access or secrets. A status log separates planned actions, actions taken and confirmed results.
Optional disclosure: Official recovery records and routes. The in-course records below support all required decisions. Live pages are optional for current real use.

prose: Ari is a fictional adult who tried to purchase a concert ticket. The incident has two confirmed exposures: a personally approved payment induced by deception, and a password entered on a false delivery page. Read the complete starting record before choosing agencies.
The sender is not independently verified. No actual address, link, telephone number or code is supplied. Knowing the amount does not explain how the sender obtained it or establish authority.

CAFC, “What to do if you're a victim of fraud,” and “Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre Impersonation”; checked September 28, 2026. Keep relevant records, promptly contact the institution that transferred money, and report fraud to local police and the official fraud/cybercrime reporting route. Recovery offers can demand fees or more information. Independently reach official services; a convincing name, document or detail from the incident is not sufficient verification. Reporting does not guarantee recovery.

Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, “Protecting yourself from identity theft online”; checked September 28, 2026. Identify the information and accounts affected, secure compromised/reused credentials and connected accounts, contact affected providers and monitor relevant activity. Choose identity-protection measures from the actual exposure or misuse, not an invented list of every possible stolen document.

CRA, “Report a scam or identity theft”; checked September 28, 2026. Suspected CRA-account compromise or unauthorized changes to CRA information, including bank or address details, warrant contacting CRA through its official reporting/support route. An unfamiliar call is not itself proof of an account change. A person can independently open the official CRA page to identify the relevant secure or telephone option. CRA account support is distinct from a CAFC report.

Service Canada, “SIN fraud and data breaches”; checked September 28, 2026; page modified May 13, 2026. Suspected SIN misuse or exposure calls for monitoring credit information and relevant accounts. The page points to both Canadian credit bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion, and explains fraud alerts and responses when fraud is identified. It says a person does not need to notify the SIN Program about suspected misuse or a breach. Issuing a new SIN is not a routine cure: the old number and its records do not simply disappear. Contact affected institutions or government programs for the misuse involving them.

heads: Start with an exposure map
Prioritize time-sensitive controls, then coordinate
Give each organization one clear job
Keep a living status log
Reject a second loss without blame
prose: List what actually left the person's control: money, a password, card details, a SIN, an identity document or device access. Then connect each item to its provider. This is more useful than a universal instruction to “call everyone.” Ari's payment belongs in a bank response; the reused credential belongs in email and music-account responses.

Separate facts from possible consequences. Ari's name and address could assist future impersonation, so continued caution matters. Those facts do not establish a new credit account or tax-account intrusion. Conversely, if a case supplies a SIN exposure and an independently observed unauthorized tax-account change, identity and CRA responses have concrete reasons. Match the measure to the evidence.

Do not postpone urgent provider contact while perfecting an evidence file. Ari already has the essential payment record and message. The bank needs prompt notice of the deceptive transfer, and exposed accounts need prompt protection through independent trusted routes. Write an order and a reason; some actions could occur close together rather than waiting days for one organization to finish.

For the connected credentials, securing the recovery email before the music account is defensible because access to that email can help reset the music account. Follow the supplied session and recovery controls as well as changing passwords. A person who has lost access may need the provider's official recovery process instead. The course cannot certify that a real account is secure.

The table supplies routes rather than memorized phone numbers. A route is independent when it comes from a trusted source already held or an official page reached without the suspicious message's link. A caller who says “use this number to verify me” is still controlling the proposed route. An official-looking logo or knowledge of an incident does not change that.

Use three columns: action planned → action taken and reference → result or next check. “Reported to bank” does not mean “money refunded.” “Changed password” does not mean every active session ended. “Subscription closed” does not mean a disputed charge was reversed. Specific status language prevents false reassurance and shows which task remains.

Record times, amounts, contact labels, categories disclosed, responses and case references. Do not put a password, SIN, full account number or one-time code into the course. Existing evidence can be kept safely; do not revisit an unsafe page or continue a scam conversation to gather more. Real institutions may have secure evidence processes; reach them independently before sharing sensitive originals.

An offer of guaranteed recovery can be attractive after a loss. That is why a recovery scam may repeat the amount, impersonate an agency and insist on a fee, code or secrecy. Ari's stranger asks for both money and an email code while discouraging the bank. Stop that interaction and preserve the existing message. The person's first mistake does not create an obligation to keep paying or to prove they deserve help.
Optional first-step hint: “Draw two branches from Ari's record: $160 → bank; reused email/music password → connected providers. Add reporting and follow-up after those controls.”

prose: I begin with the financial fact: Ari approved the transfer under deceptive circumstances. I do not call it an unapproved transaction, and I do not assume a deposited transfer can simply be cancelled. I direct prompt notice to the bank through its genuine app, using the separate device.

Next I connect the email and music accounts. Both use the entered password, and the email is a recovery path for music. The provider guide tells me to handle sessions separately. The stranger's knowledge of $160 does not verify the offer; the proposed $40 payment and email code would create further exposure.
Complete coordinated plan:

The unsupported shortcut is “CAFC will recover everything; wait for its answer.” It leaves the bank and exposed credentials unattended and invents a result. Coordination means several specific jobs, each with a relevant recipient.

heads: Nico's identity and account-response file
prose: Nico is a fictional 19-year-old. This new case has no ticket transfer and no entered account password. Prepare a coordinated identity-response plan from the supplied records.

Document E — Job-form exposure, October 21, 2026, 9:00 a.m. Nico submitted a supposed employer's onboarding form before any interview or verified job offer. It requested and received Nico's full name, date of birth, mailing address, SIN and bank direct-deposit routing/account details. The actual numbers are omitted. Nico did not enter any bank/email/CRA password, card number, PIN or one-time code, upload an identity-document image, install an app or grant remote access. No money was sent. Nico later independently reached the named employer through its known public office and learned it had no such application or offer. The saved form summary and messages are available without reopening the false form.

Document F — Independently observed records, October 21, 10:00 a.m. Nico opened the genuine bank app and the official CRA account using a separate updated personal device and previously established sign-in routes. The bank showed no unfamiliar transaction at that time. The CRA account showed direct-deposit information changed that morning to an account Nico does not recognize and did not request. The actual account digits are omitted. How the change was made is unknown. Nico can still access the account. No CRA support report or bank notification has yet occurred. No credit reports have yet been reviewed; no new credit account is confirmed.

Document G — Recovery message, 10:10 a.m. An unverified sender claims to be a national fraud-recovery officer and requests a $65 “identity reset” fee plus a CRA one-time sign-in code. The sender promises to erase all identity records and tells Nico not to contact CRA. No referral to this person appears in any independently reached official record. Nico has not paid or sent a code.

Document H — Routes and evidence available. Nico has the genuine bank app's security/support contact, the official CRA report-scam/identity-theft page, the official Service Canada SIN fraud/data-breach page with its links to Equifax and TransUnion, the official local police site, and CAFC's official victim-response page linking to Report Cybercrime and Fraud. These are independently reached official resources, represented by the dated source records in this lesson. No live visit is needed. The evidence set includes the job messages, form summary with sensitive numbers safely excluded from this exercise, independent employer verification, the observed CRA-change record, bank observation time and recovery message. There is no result from an investigation yet.

No password, card data, PIN, code, ID image, app installation, remote access or payment is supplied. At 10:00 a.m., the genuine CRA account showed an unauthorized direct-deposit change; its mechanism and any diverted payment are unknown. The bank showed no unfamiliar transaction at that observation time. Credit reports have not been checked, so no new credit account is established. These are stronger identity-misuse concerns than name exposure alone. Stop interacting with the false employer and recovery sender. Promptly contact CRA through the independently reached Canada.ca report-scam/identity-theft route because an actual unauthorized CRA change is visible. Describe the observation and seek its account-protection, identity and correction instructions; do not assume a CAFC report performs those controls. Promptly notify the bank through its genuine app's security/support route about the exposed direct-deposit details and identity information, even though no unfamiliar transaction was visible at 10:00. Ask what monitoring and account protections fit that exposure, and follow its instructions rather than claiming the bank password or card was stolen. Use the official Service Canada SIN page's links to both Equifax and TransUnion to review credit information and ask about fraud alerts appropriate to this SIN exposure and observed identity misuse. Investigate and dispute any unfamiliar credit activity through the relevant bureau and creditor if it appears. A fraud alert is an additional verification measure, not a guarantee that every account is locked. Follow the current SIN page: suspected misuse does not require notifying the SIN Program or routinely getting a new SIN. Contact the affected program—CRA here—for the misuse involving it. Do not infer that a new SIN would erase the old records. Report the suspected fraud/identity misuse to local police through the independently reached official local route and to the CAFC-linked Report Cybercrime and Fraud service. Retain report references and give consistent facts. A privacy-safe log begins: “October 21: 9:00 false onboarding form received name, birth date, address, SIN and direct-deposit details; no passwords/codes/payment. Employer independently denied application/offer. 10:00 genuine CRA account showed unrequested bank-detail change; bank app showed no unfamiliar transaction at that time. 10:10 unverified recovery sender demanded $65 and CRA code; neither supplied.” Retain the already available messages, safe form summary, employer verification and account observations; append actual provider actions, references and results without putting the numbers or code into the course. Do not pay $65, send a code or follow the stranger's contact route. A claimed agency title and an “identity reset” promise do not establish authority. Continue monitoring the bank, CRA information and credit records through trusted routes and follow official provider instructions. An unfamiliar credit account would add contact with that creditor and bureau; an unfamiliar bank transaction would require prompt bank reporting; an uncorrected CRA change would require CRA follow-up. No refund, clean identity record, recovered payment or completed investigation is established. The plan can prioritize CRA and bank actions close together; a different order is acceptable if it explains both urgent exposures and does not postpone them for a general report.
